title: Overview & setup
description: What EMBERBench measures, installation and a first evaluation.
text: EMBERBench EMBERBench is a benchmark for decision-making models on dynamic fire-evacuation tasks. A model controls the people in a 2D grid building. Fire spreads through the building, and the model must decide each timestep how every person moves. The benchmark measures how well the model's decisions get people out through the exits before the fire reaches them. Status: V1 release candidate, benchmark revision 2, not yet released (package 0.1.0). This repository contains the benchmark contract, the deterministic simulation core, the frozen V1 fairness and semantics specification, the matched stochastic hazard contract, auditable per-episode metrics, crowd coordination diagnostics, the canonical V1 public scenario suite, paired evaluation on exact scenario + seed schedules, deterministic statistics, reference baselines, the procedural generator (1.1, ten V1 scenario families) and the suite-composition rules, the hidden-test integrity protocol, the emberbench CLI, replay audit and visualization, the official EMBER Score and frozen environment packs. The public suite is for development and diagnostics; scored V1 evaluation uses a held-out generated suite. Wind, delayed ignitions, burn-out, smoke and material flammability are deferred to a future benchmark version. LLM provider integrations, a UI and human-behaviour models are out of scope. What EMBERBench measures The benchmark looks at the quality of sequential decisions under a changing hazard: routing people to exits that are reachable and that stay usable, avoiding routes that the fire will cut off, managing congestion at corridors and exits, reacting when the fire makes an exit unusable. Per-episode raw metrics (evacuated, casualties, stranded, timing, congestion, path efficiency, a fire-exposure proxy, exit use and replanning proxies) are computed from the Scenario and the RunRecord with compute_episode_metrics. It scores only records that pass structural validation and a full simulator replay (verify_record). See docs/metrics.md. The metrics have no single score: raw metrics are canonical, and safety always comes before speed. Crowd coordination diagnostics come from compute_crowd_diagnostics on the same authenticated inputs: per-step movement and block counts, contested cells, a row-major table of congestion hotspots, per-exit throughput and a static nearest-exit demand proxy. They observe the frozen V1 crowd rules and do not model human behaviour. See docs/crowd-diagnostics.md. build_replay_audit turns the same authenticated inputs into a read-only replay audit: a step-by-step timeline, per-person paths, per-step fire deltas and an optional congestion overlay. Deterministic ASCII frames (render_frame) and a portable JSON animation export (export_animation) come from that audit. Visualization never affects benchmark results. See docs/replay-visualization.md. Five deterministic, non-LLM reference baselines (random legal, nearest-exit greedy, static shortest-path, fire-aware shortest-path and congestion-aware routing) run through the same model interface as any evaluated model and see only the observation. Reference baselines are anchors, not benchmark winners. A separate, privileged escape bound gives an evaluator-side upper bound on evacuations. See docs/baselines.md. Fairness principle Every compared model runs on exactly the same episode: the same scenario: map, obstacles, exits, initial population (with stable person IDs), ignition points and hazard configuration, the same simulator version and rules, the same evaluator seed schedule, and therefore the same exogenous fire process. The evaluator seed is for reproducibility and matched evaluation only. A model never receives the seed, the RNG state, future random draws or hidden scenario metadata. A model receives only the model-visible Observation: the current step, the static map, the episode rules (fire model and parameters, fire-entry policy, conflict rule, step limit), the people, the burning cells and the allowed actions. V1 evaluates decisions under known rules; only the evaluator randomness is hidden. Fire is exogenous in V1: actions do not change it. For the same scenario and seed, every model faces the same fire trajectory, so a difference in outcome comes from the decisions only. Model outputs are the only thing that differs between two matched runs. The normative contract is in docs/v1-fairness-spec.md. Deterministic scenario + seed evaluation A (scenario, seed) pair fully defines a benchmark episode. The seed belongs to the evaluator, not to the model: All randomness comes from simulator-owned SplitMix64 streams. Each stream is derived from the seed and a subsystem label (for example fire). The code does not use random, the clock, UUIDs or any global state. Iteration over sets and dicts is always sorted first, so results do not depend on PYTHONHASHSEED. A test checks this across processes. The same scenario, seed and action sequence produce byte-identical canonical JSON run records. verify_record() replays a stored run and rejects any mismatch. It also rejects a different scenario hash, a different SIMULATOR_VERSION or a different OBSERVATION_VERSION. Development scenarios are not the test set The scenarios in tests/fixtures/scenarios/ are tiny test fixtures. They exist to check simulator behaviour. They are not benchmark scoring scenarios, and they are not intended to become the final hidden test set. The scored evaluation set must be kept separate from development scenarios, so that models cannot be tuned to it. Canonical V1 public suite scenarios/public/v1/ holds the fixed, public V1 diagnostic suite (emberbench-v1-public, suite version 1.0.0): ten scenarios that cover twelve diagnostic families, from a sparse single-exit room to a 100-person crowd and a stochastic route invalidation. A manifest pins each scenario's content hash. load_suite() verifies the manifest against the files. The suite is public by design. It is not the hidden evaluation set, and its seeds are development defaults, not evaluator seeds. See docs/scenario-suite.md. from emberbench import load_suite suite = load_suite("scenarios/public/v1") for scenario in suite.scenarios: print(scenario.scenario_id, scenario.content_hash()) Procedural unseen scenarios generate_suite() builds unseen V1 scenarios from a public GeneratorConfig and an evaluator-private generator seed, with no ambient entropy. Every scenario must meet explicit generation constraints (route existence, passage width, route redundancy, densities, exit separation, ignition distances), or generation fails. freeze_generated_suite() writes the suite once, before any model runs, and load_generated_suite() verifies it and returns a normal Suite for build_evaluation_manifest() and run_evaluation(). The seed is never stored. See docs/procedural-generation.md. emberbench.composition composes the V1 evaluation suite from a generated candidate pool on the evaluator side: unique worlds, the frozen calibration panel, admission, difficulty band, the ten V1 family rules, deterministic family x band x fire-model quotas with targeted top-up, and a private freeze record. See docs/generator.md. Hidden-test integrity emberbench.integrity defines the held-out protocol: which assets are public and which stay with the evaluator, an evaluator workspace outside the repository, a provider-neutral SubmissionIdentity, and an immutable EvaluationProvenance record that pins the versions, the frozen suite, the evaluation manifest hash, the submission and the result digest by SHA-256. It holds no seeds and no timestamps. Signatures are optional and external. verify_evaluation_provenance() re-derives every pin and fails closed. Post-submission generation binds the generator seed to a frozen submission roster. emberbench.leakguard keeps held-out material out of the repository, the wheel and the sdist. Hashes prove content identity, not authorship. See docs/integrity.md. The EMBER Score score_results(trials, pack) gives one failure-sensitive number in [0, 100]: benchmark-performance points under EMBER scoring version 1.0, never a percentage of people evacuated. It is 100 * Safety * Quality^beta * Severity. Safety multiplies evacuation, a casualty factor and a stranding factor over losses attributed person by person (a loss is avoidable when that person could have escaped), and is 0 when half of the savable people are lost. Quality is a weighted geometric mean of time, hazard, path and replanning, each relative to a privileged optimum of the same episode; time is relative to a capacity bound that counts unavoidable queues at exits and doors. Every input is a function of the replayed state trajectory, so identical trajectories score identically. Congestion (block rate, contested cells, hotspots, exit throughput) is reported in every score report but is never a score input: a bottleneck is charged by the delay, exposure and losses it causes. An avoidable casualty caps an episode below 60; a severe delay (including a severe realized bottleneck), exposure, path or replanning failure caps it below 80. Missing, invalid, failed and timed-out episodes score 0 and are counted. Episodes are averaged by scenario, then by primary family; the report gives a stratified bootstrap 95% interval, every component, per-family scores and lower-tail statistics. compare_scores gives a paired outcome (a_better, b_better, inconclusive or exact_tie), and leaderboard_order breaks ties by safety. Every model is scored on the same frozen EnvironmentPack (freeze_environment_pack, verify_environment_pack), whose digest pins the scenario bytes, the seed schedule, the versions and the fire world of every episode. See docs/scoring.md, docs/environment-pack.md and the research and sensitivity study in docs/benchmark-methodology.md. V1 scope Area V1 behaviour World 2D grid. Cells: empty, wall/obstacle, exit, fire, person. People One cell each. Stable unique IDs. One move per step (N/S/E/W/stay). No panic, health, groups or speed differences. Collisions Deterministic and documented. The lowest ID wins a contested cell. Swaps and rotations are blocked. Following another person in the same step is allowed. Exits Entering a non-burning exit evacuates the person in the same step. Each exit cell lets one person through per step. Fire Spreads to 4-neighbours. It never passes through walls. Model: deterministic or seeded stochastic. exits_flammable is explicit in config. No burn-out. Casualties An active person on a burning cell becomes a casualty. Moving into fire is either blocked or a casualty (config). Termination all_resolved (nobody is active) or max_steps. The full rules are in docs/simulation-contract.md. The frozen V1 decisions and their rationale are in docs/v1-fairness-spec.md. The scenario file format is in docs/scenario-schema.md. Deterministic phase order (per timestep) Observation (state snapshot before the step) Submitted movement actions (validated, exactly one per active person) Movement validation (boundary, wall, fire policy) Collision and congestion resolution Person movement (simultaneous) Evacuation through exits Fire propagation Casualties and trapping updates Termination check Paired evaluation An EvaluationManifest pins an ordered schedule of (scenario, seed) episodes, the suite hash and the simulator, observation and metrics versions. Every model runs the same manifest, so all models face the same fire (common random numbers). run_evaluation() builds a fresh policy per episode, gives it only Observation values, saves an authenticated per-model artifact after every episode and resumes it after an interruption. pair_results() reports exactly which episodes two artifacts can compare. The seeds come from the evaluator; this repository does not generate scored seeds. See docs/evaluation.md. from emberbench import build_evaluation_manifest, load_suite, pair_results, run_evaluation suite = load_suite("scenarios/public/v1") manifest = build_evaluation_manifest(suite, [3, 1, 4]) # development seeds only a = run_evaluation(suite, manifest, "model-a", make_policy_a, "model-a.json") b = run_evaluation(suite, manifest, "model-b", make_policy_b, "model-b.json") print(pair_results(a, b).paired_count) Architecture src/emberbench/ scenario.py versioned scenario schema, strict parsing and validation, content hash grid.py positions, cell kinds, actions, neighbourhoods rng.py simulation-owned SplitMix64 streams, seed derivation fire.py FireModel protocol, deterministic and stochastic spread movement.py action parsing, movement validation, collision resolution state.py immutable, evaluator-private SimState snapshots, render() observation.py the versioned model-visible Observation, MapView and RulesView simulator.py Simulator: runs the 9 phases, run_episode() events.py StepRecord / RunRecord, the replay and audit log replay.py replay() and verify_record() metrics.py compute_episode_metrics(): auditable raw per-episode metrics crowd.py compute_crowd_diagnostics(): congestion, hotspots, exit load signals baselines.py fair reference baseline agents and their registry oracle.py PRIVILEGED evaluator-side escape bound (not a model) suite.py scenario suite manifests: strict parsing, load_suite() verification evaluation.py evaluation manifests, run_evaluation() with resume, pair_results() integrity.py held-out protocol: asset classes, submission identity, provenance, verification leakguard.py path allowlist and leak checks for the repository, wheel and sdist canonical.py canonical JSON and SHA-256 hashing cli.py the `emberbench` command line (also `python -m emberbench`) errors.py explicit exception types The concepts stay separate. The scenario is static input. The simulator owns the mutable run and produces immutable state snapshots. Fire dynamics and movement resolution are pure functions of their inputs (and of the passed RNG stream). Events record what happened. Metrics (metrics.py) use the Scenario and the RunRecord together. Some metrics need the static map or the configuration from the scenario, so not every metric can come from RunRecord alone. Minimal use from emberbench import Simulator, load_scenario scenario = load_scenario("tests/fixtures/scenarios/one_person_one_exit.json") sim = Simulator(scenario) # or Simulator(scenario, seed=123) while not sim.done: obs = sim.observe() # phase 1: the only thing a model may see sim.step({p.id: "east" for p in obs.active}) record = sim.record() # replayable, canonical RunRecord print(record.final_state.termination_reason, record.digest()) Replay and events A RunRecord holds everything needed to replay and audit a run: simulator_version, observation_version, schema_version, scenario_id, scenario_hash, seed initial_state for each step: the submitted actions, the resolved movements (intent, final cell and outcome such as moved or blocked_conflict), the ignited cells, the evacuations (person and exit), the casualties (person, cell and cause), and the full post-step state (people, burning cells, trapped set, RNG position and termination). All records serialise to canonical JSON (record.to_json()) and load back with no loss (RunRecord.from_json). Command-line interface The package installs an emberbench command (also python -m emberbench). It is a thin, deterministic, provider-free front end to the library: no network access, no ambient configuration, no generated seeds and no implicit code loading. emberbench suite validate scenarios/public/v1 emberbench evaluation manifest --suite scenarios/public/v1 --seed 0 --seed 1 --seed 2 --out manifest.json emberbench evaluation run --suite scenarios/public/v1 --manifest manifest.json --model-id my-model --agent my_agents:make_agent --agent-path . --out result.json Every command supports --json, refuses to overwrite files and exits with a stable code. See docs/cli.md. Running the tests Requires Python 3.12+ and has no runtime dependencies. The development tools are pinned in tools/dev-constraints.txt, the same versions CI uses. python -m pip install -c tools/dev-constraints.txt -e ".[dev]" python -m pytest python -m mypy python tools/check_public_assets.py The suite covers deterministic replay, two independent simulator instances, cross-process PYTHONHASHSEED independence, serialisation round trips, walls blocking movement and fire, exit behaviour, explicit rejection of invalid scenarios and actions, collision rules, termination, ID stability, golden trajectory digests, every frozen V1 rule, the observation contract (no seed, RNG state or hidden metadata), the fire trajectory invariance across different actions, and the canonical public suite (pinned hashes, strict manifest checks and per-scenario diagnostic properties), and paired evaluation (manifest hashing, seed privacy, fresh policies per episode, identical fire across models, resume and tamper rejection, exact pairing), and the stochastic hazard contract (exact ignition probability, one draw per frontier edge, matched fire across policies and pinned cross-platform golden fire traces), and crowd diagnostics (the frozen queue and throughput rules, exact reconciliation with the run record and the metrics, hotspots in the public crowd scenarios, 50/100/200-person stress runs and golden diagnostic digests). Any change to simulator output fails the golden test until you bump SIMULATOR_VERSION on purpose. Versions and releases The package version (emberbench.__version__), the benchmark revision (BENCHMARK_REVISION) and the component contract versions are separate; emberbench version --json reports all of them. The rules are in docs/versioning.md, the history in docs/changelog.md and the release steps, including the regression digest registry and tools/check_release.py, in docs/release-checklist.md. License EMBERBench is licensed under the Apache License 2.0 (Apache-2.0); see LICENSE. The license covers the benchmark implementation, the public suite and the protocol in this repository. Hidden evaluation suites are never part of this repository (docs/integrity.md).

title: Command line
description: Commands, arguments and repeatable workflows.
text:
Command-line interface CLI_VERSION = "1.0" The emberbench command exposes the library contracts as a deterministic, provider-free command line. Every command calls the existing library API (load_scenario, load_suite, load_generated_suite, build_evaluation_manifest, run_episode, verify_record, run_evaluation, load_evaluation_result, aggregate_result, compare_results). The CLI adds argument parsing, fail-closed input loading, no-overwrite atomic output and stable exit codes. It does not add a second simulator, a second validator or a second artifact format. The CLI uses only the standard library (argparse). Entry points emberbench version --json python -m emberbench version --json Both run the same function, emberbench.cli:main. The console script is installed by the package ([project.scripts] in pyproject.toml). python -m normally puts the current directory first on sys.path. The module entry point removes it, so the current directory never decides which agent code is imported (see Agent factories). Command tree emberbench version contract versions scenario validate FILE one scenario file suite validate DIR a suite directory (manifest.json + scenario files) generated validate DIR a frozen generated suite (generation.json + suite/) evaluation manifest build an EvaluationManifest from a suite and ordered seeds evaluation run run every manifest episode with a local agent (resumable) evaluation verify authenticate an EvaluationResult episode run run one scenario with one seed and a local agent replay verify authenticate one RunRecord by replay statistics aggregate AggregateStatistics of one result statistics compare PairedStatistics of two results (A - B) Every command accepts: --json: print only the result, as one canonical JSON line on stdout. --debug: print a Python traceback to stderr on failure. --help: print the usage of the command. Options go after the command words (emberbench suite validate DIR --json). Option names are never abbreviated. Commands that take a suite accept exactly one of: --suite DIR: a suite directory, loaded with load_suite. --generated-suite DIR: a frozen generated suite, loaded with load_generated_suite. The freeze record is checked as well. Commands version emberbench version --json Prints the package version (package_version, from src/emberbench/_version.py, see versioning.md) and every contract version of this build: benchmark_revision and every benchmark-defining version, exactly the entries of benchmark_versions() that evaluation provenance pins: simulator_version, observation_version, action_schema_version, schema_version (the scenario schema), metrics_version, crowd_diagnostics_version, statistics_version, generator_version, generator_config_version, generation_manifest_version, evaluation_manifest_version, evaluation_result_version, scoring_version, environment_pack_version, environment_world_version, family_rules_version, calibration_panel_version, difficulty_rules_version, admission_rules_version, composition_version, selection_rules_version, recipe_catalog_version and suite_freeze_record_version; the tooling contracts that do not change what a score means: cli_version, baselines_version, integrity_protocol_version, replay_audit_version and animation_format_version. The benchmark-defining part is built from benchmark_versions(), so a version that provenance pins is always reported (see versioning.md, section 3, and docs/integrity.md, section 12). No field depends on the environment (no paths, platform, interpreter or install location). These keys were added before any release, so CLI_VERSION stays 1.0. scenario validate FILE emberbench scenario validate scenarios/public/v1/v1-pub-01-single-exit-sparse.json --json Loads the file with the strict scenario parser. Reports scenario_id, scenario_hash (the content hash) and schema_version. suite validate DIR emberbench suite validate scenarios/public/v1 --json Loads the suite with load_suite: every listed file must exist, no file may be unlisted, and every pinned hash and derived field must match. Reports suite_id, suite_version, suite_hash, visibility, seed_role, schema_version, scenario_count and scenarios (each scenario_id and content_hash, in manifest order). generated validate DIR emberbench generated validate path/to/frozen-batch --json Loads a frozen generated suite with load_generated_suite and checks the freeze record against every scenario. Reports the suite fields above and generation_manifest_version, generator_version, batch_id and config_hash. The private generator seed is not in the freeze record, so it is never shown. evaluation manifest emberbench evaluation manifest --suite scenarios/public/v1 --seed 1 --seed 7 --seed 42 --out manifest.json Builds the manifest with build_evaluation_manifest(suite, seeds) and writes its canonical file text (EvaluationManifest.to_file_text(), the bytes that save_evaluation_manifest writes). --seed N is repeatable and required. The order is kept exactly. The CLI never generates, sorts or removes seeds. A seed is a decimal integer in [0, 2**64 - 1]. A duplicate seed is a usage error. --out FILE is required. --force replaces an existing file. Reports manifest_hash, manifest_version, the suite fields, episode_count and seed_count. The seed values are never printed: they stay in the file the operator asked for. episode run emberbench episode run --scenario scenarios/public/v1/v1-pub-01-single-exit-sparse.json --seed 3 --agent my_agents:make_agent --out record.json Runs one episode through the single simulator path: run_episode(scenario, agent_policy(agent), seed=SEED). The agent is built fresh with the factory, receives only Observation values and its output is validated by validate_actions. The record is then checked with verify_record and written as canonical JSON plus one LF (RunRecord.to_json() + "
"). --scenario FILE, --seed N, --agent MODULE:FACTORY and --out FILE are required. The scenario file's development seed is not used. --agent-path DIR (repeatable) and --force are optional. Reports scenario_id, scenario_hash, simulator_version, observation_version, record_digest, steps and termination_reason. replay verify emberbench replay verify --scenario scenarios/public/v1/v1-pub-01-single-exit-sparse.json --record record.json --json The record file must be JSON that RunRecord.from_dict accepts and that round-trips exactly (no unknown or changed fields). Otherwise: exit 3. verify_record(scenario, record) replays the action log. Any version, scenario-hash, initial-state or trajectory difference: exit 5. validate_run_record(scenario, record) requires a complete, well-formed episode. A replayable prefix that stops before termination: exit 3. Reports verified: true, scenario_id, scenario_hash, record_digest, simulator_version, observation_version, steps and termination_reason. There is no best-effort recovery. evaluation run emberbench evaluation run --suite scenarios/public/v1 --manifest manifest.json --model-id my-model --agent my_agents:make_agent --out result.json Calls run_evaluation(suite, manifest, model_id, agent_policy_factory(factory), out, resume=...) unchanged. Every episode gets a new agent. --manifest FILE, --model-id ID, --agent MODULE:FACTORY and --out FILE are required. --model-id must pass the library model ID check (non-empty, printable, at most 256 characters, no outer whitespace). An existing --out file is never overwritten. Without --resume it is an output conflict (exit 6). With --resume it must load and authenticate completely and carry the same manifest hash and model ID (otherwise exit 3 or 6). Completed episodes are not run again. This is the library resume behaviour; the CLI does not change it. run_evaluation saves the artifact atomically after every episode. If the agent fails, the last checkpoint stays on disk so that --resume can continue it. This is the only command that leaves an artifact behind after a failure, and that artifact is always a complete, valid checkpoint. Reports model_id, result_version, manifest_hash, the suite fields, result_digest, scheduled_episodes, completed_episodes and complete. evaluation verify emberbench evaluation verify --suite scenarios/public/v1 --result result.json --manifest manifest.json --require-complete --json Calls load_evaluation_result(result, suite): the embedded manifest must match the suite and the running versions, and every episode's run record is authenticated by replay and its metrics are recomputed. A malformed, duplicate, unknown, non-canonical or tampered episode fails the whole artifact (exit 3, or exit 5 when the cause is a replay mismatch). No episode is dropped or repaired. --manifest FILE also requires this exact evaluation manifest (exit 5 if the embedded manifest differs). --require-complete also requires every scheduled episode (exit 5 if any is missing). Without it, a partial result that authenticates is valid. Reports verified: true and the same fields as evaluation run. statistics aggregate emberbench statistics aggregate --suite scenarios/public/v1 --result result.json --out stats.json Loads and authenticates the result, then writes aggregate_result(result, suite).to_json() + "
". statistics compare emberbench statistics compare --suite scenarios/public/v1 --a a.json --b b.json --out paired.json Loads and authenticates both results, then writes compare_results(a, b, suite).to_json() + "
". Deltas are A - B. Results of different manifests are rejected. Both statistics commands accept --resamples N. Without it the library default (DEFAULT_BOOTSTRAP_RESAMPLES, 2000) is used: the CLI does not pass the argument at all. Out-of-range values are a usage error. They report statistics_version, digest (the artifact's digest()), the model IDs, manifest_hash and resamples. Exit codes Code Name Meaning 0 OK Success. 1 INTERNAL Unexpected failure (a bug). Rerun with --debug for a traceback. 2 USAGE Malformed command line or argument value: unknown command or option, missing option, bad seed, duplicate seed, bad --resamples, bad --model-id, malformed --agent, missing --agent-path directory. 3 VALIDATION An input is missing, unreadable, not JSON, malformed, not canonical, tampered, incomplete where completeness is required, or fails a library check (ScenarioValidationError, SuiteValidationError, GenerationError, EvaluationError, StatisticsInputError, MetricsInputError). 4 AGENT The agent module cannot be imported, the factory is missing or not callable, the factory raises or returns a non-agent or a reused agent, act raises, or the model output is rejected (ModelOutputError). 5 MISMATCH A replay does not reproduce the record (ReplayMismatchError, also when it is the cause of another error), or an evaluation result does not match the required manifest or completeness. 6 OUTPUT The output file exists (without --force or --resume), is a directory, is also an input file, its parent directory does not exist, or it cannot be written. 130 INTERRUPTED Interrupted (KeyboardInterrupt). The codes are emberbench.cli.ExitCode and are pinned by tests. A Python traceback is never printed unless --debug is given. Output JSON mode (--json) On success, stdout holds exactly one line: the result object as canonical JSON (sorted keys, no whitespace, ASCII). Nothing else is printed to stdout. Every result has a command field. Results never include input or output paths, timestamps, hostnames or environment details. On failure, stdout is empty and stderr holds exactly one line: {"error":{"exit_code":N,"kind":"...","message":"..."}}. With --debug the traceback follows on stderr. There are no ANSI escape codes or colours. Usage errors found while parsing the command line, before the command is known, are also reported in this JSON form when --json is present. Human mode A short key: value list on stdout. Errors go to stderr as emberbench: error: MESSAGE. Error messages are deterministic for the same inputs. Library messages can contain the input paths as given on the command line. Files Inputs are never written Validation, verification and statistics commands only read their inputs. An output path that is the same file as an input is refused, even with --force. Output rules An existing output file is never replaced unless --force is given. evaluation run has no --force: an existing result can only be resumed. Parent directories are never created. A missing parent is exit 6. The output is written to a temporary file in the same directory, flushed and fsynced. With --force the temporary file is then renamed over the output (os.replace). Without --force it is hard-linked to the output path. The link fails if the file exists, so a file that another process creates in the meantime is never replaced either. If the filesystem has no hard links, the CLI creates the output with O_CREAT | O_EXCL (this also fails if the file exists), writes the bytes, flushes and fsyncs. On such a filesystem the output is visible while it is written. If that write fails, the CLI removes the file, but only if it is still the file that the CLI created. There is never a check-then-replace step. On any failure, no output file and no temporary file are left behind (evaluation run checkpoints are the documented exception above). Inputs are validated and the output path is checked before an agent is imported or an episode runs. Artifact bytes Command File content evaluation manifest EvaluationManifest.to_file_text() (indented JSON, LF) episode run RunRecord.to_json() + "
" evaluation run EvaluationResult.to_file_text() (written by run_evaluation) statistics aggregate AggregateStatistics.to_json() + "
" statistics compare PairedStatistics.to_json() + "
" All artifacts are ASCII with LF line endings on every platform. They hold no absolute paths and no timestamps. A record or statistics digest is the SHA-256 of the file without its final LF. Agent factories episode run and evaluation run import the operator's agent code. This is the only place where the CLI imports code that is not part of EMBERBench, and it happens only when --agent is given. --agent MODULE:FACTORY MODULE is a dotted Python module path (my_pkg.agents). FACTORY is an attribute path in that module (make_agent or Agents.make). Both parts use ASCII identifiers only. Anything else is a usage error (exit 2). The CLI imports exactly MODULE with importlib.import_module and reads FACTORY from it. There is no entry-point discovery, plugin registry, fallback module, network location or search of the current directory. The module must be importable from sys.path as the interpreter sets it, or from a directory given explicitly with --agent-path DIR (repeatable; the directories are put first, in the order given, for this command only). The factory must satisfy the AgentFactory contract (docs/model-interface.md): It is a zero-argument callable. Every call returns a new object with an act(observation) method. A returned agent that was already used for an earlier episode is rejected. act receives only the Observation. It never receives the scenario, seed, manifest, episode index or run record. Example agent module: # my_agents.py from emberbench import Action, PolicyAgent def make_agent(): return PolicyAgent(lambda obs: {p.id: Action.STAY for p in obs.active}) emberbench episode run --scenario scenarios/public/v1/v1-pub-01-single-exit-sparse.json --seed 3 --agent my_agents:make_agent --agent-path . --out record.json Importing a module runs its code. Use --agent only with code that you trust. Configuration, determinism and network policy There is no configuration file, no home-directory configuration, no .env file and no environment variable that changes a result. Every value that affects a benchmark result comes from an explicit argument, an explicit input file or a versioned library default. The current directory does not change results. Relative paths are resolved against it, as usual, and nothing else is taken from it. The same command with the same input files gives byte-identical output files and stdout, under any PYTHONHASHSEED, from any current directory and on Linux, Windows and macOS. The order of options does not matter. The order of --seed options does: it is the manifest order. The CLI core never opens a network connection: it does not download models, contact providers, check for updates or fetch URLs. A test runs every command under an audit hook that fails on any socket or URL event. An agent that the operator loads with --agent may use the network itself. That is outside the CLI core and is the operator's explicit choice. Examples (public development assets) emberbench suite validate scenarios/public/v1 emberbench evaluation manifest --suite scenarios/public/v1 --seed 0 --seed 1 --seed 2 --out manifest.json --json emberbench evaluation run --suite scenarios/public/v1 --manifest manifest.json --model-id stay --agent my_agents:make_agent --agent-path . --out stay.json emberbench evaluation verify --suite scenarios/public/v1 --result stay.json --manifest manifest.json --require-complete emberbench statistics aggregate --suite scenarios/public/v1 --result stay.json --out stay-stats.json The public seeds 0, 1, 2 give the evaluation manifest hash 7b9aae45e5e2828f881b2f14d8e5585627e5f8bdbb137a1ed2331bf10ce8c876. Development seeds are for development only; scored seed schedules belong to the evaluator (docs/evaluation.md).

title: Model interface
description: Observations, actions and the decision-model contract.
text: Model interface This document specifies the provider-independent boundary between EMBERBench and a decision model. Planners, LLMs, RL agents and future external adapters all run through the same boundary: Observation -> {person_id: Action} The code is in src/emberbench/agent.py. The tests are in tests/test_agent.py. The interface adds no runtime dependency, no async API and no network API. It does not change the simulator rules, the Observation fields, the evaluation manifest, paired seed semantics or the result artifact. No version is bumped. Out of scope here: provider integrations (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini and others), agent frameworks and RL libraries. The reference baseline agents (Issue #10) use this interface unchanged; see baselines.md. 1. Model-visible input A model receives exactly one value per timestep: an Observation (observation version 1.0, see v1-fairness-spec.md). It contains: Field Content step the current step number, from 0 map grid width and height, obstacles, exits (ID and position) rules fire model, spread interval and probability, exit flammability, enter-fire policy, conflict resolution, max_steps people every person: ID, position and status (active, evacuated, casualty) burning every burning cell allowed_actions stay, north, south, east, west The model never receives: the Scenario, its ID, description, content hash or development seed, the evaluator seed, the EvaluationManifest, an episode entry or index, the Simulator, SimState, RunRecord or result artifact, RNG state (stream seeds or positions) or future draws, the trapped diagnostic, metrics or other evaluator metadata. The current state is fully observable and the rules are known. The data above is evaluator-private because it either determines the future (seed, RNG state) or identifies the episode (scenario ID, hash, index). A model that saw it could memorize or predict the stochastic fire instead of reacting to the observed state. The trapped diagnostic is a computed answer that the model must find itself. Keeping all of it outside the interface keeps paired comparisons fair. 2. Expected output act returns a mapping from person ID to action: exactly one entry for every active person (observation.active), no entry for an unknown person or for an evacuated or casualty person, each value an Action member or its string value ("north"), which is what the simulator accepts, and a member of observation.allowed_actions. The static types say the same thing: ActionValue = Action | str # Action.NORTH or "north" ActionOutput = Mapping[str, ActionValue] # person ID -> action value Agent.act, PolicyAgent.act, validate_actions and serialize_actions use these types. The static type does not weaken the runtime check: a string that is not an action value ("up", "NORTH") is still rejected. A move that cannot happen (into a wall, out of the grid, into an occupied cell) is still a legal action. The simulator resolves it to a blocked_* outcome. The interface does not judge the quality of an action. 3. Interface types class Agent(Protocol): def act(self, observation: Observation) -> ActionOutput: ... AgentFactory = Callable[[], Agent] # called once per episode, no arguments Name Purpose Agent a decision model for one episode AgentFactory builds a new agent; receives no arguments PolicyAgent(policy) adapts a stateless Observation -> actions callable to Agent validate_actions(obs, output) checks model output; returns a new dict[str, Action] agent_policy(agent) binds one agent to one episode; returns a simulator Policy agent_policy_factory(factory) a run_evaluation policy factory that builds a new agent per episode ExecutionMetadata, StepExecution, ReportsExecution optional accounting (section 7) serialize_observation, deserialize_observation, observation_from_dict canonical observation text (section 8) ACTION_SCHEMA_VERSION, serialize_actions, deserialize_actions canonical action payload (section 9) The three adapter shapes map onto these types: Synchronous callable policy: PolicyAgent(greedy_policy). The callable is shared between episodes, so it must be stateless. Stateful per-episode agent: a class with act, built by the factory, for example agent_policy_factory(MyPlanner). Future external or remote adapter: a class with act that sends serialize_observation(observation) to the model, parses the reply with deserialize_actions(observation, reply) and optionally implements last_execution(). Remote calls, retries and timeouts live inside the adapter (section 6.1). The core stays synchronous. 4. Episode lifecycle run_evaluation(suite, manifest, model_id, agent_policy_factory(factory), path) runs this lifecycle for each episode: Construct. factory() is called with no arguments. Construction is the reset: an agent starts clean. There is no separate reset method. Act. agent.act(observation) is called once per timestep, in step order from step 0, until the episode terminates. Each result is validated before the simulator sees it. Discard. After the episode the agent is dropped. It is never used again. Rules that make this hold: A policy from agent_policy accepts the steps of one episode only. An observation with an unexpected step number (a second episode, or a skipped step) raises EvaluationError. agent_policy_factory raises EvaluationError if the factory returns an object without a callable act, or any agent that it returned for an earlier episode (A -> A and A -> B -> A are both rejected). Reuse is detected by identity, not equality: the factory keeps a strong reference to every agent it returned, so each id() stays unique for its lifetime. Prior agents are therefore kept alive until the factory is dropped; correctness comes first. Use one agent_policy_factory(...) per evaluation run. 5. State isolation A new agent is built for every episode, so state that an agent keeps cannot carry into the next episode. This is the same fresh-policy-per-episode guarantee as in evaluation.md section 4, and it keeps resume correct: an episode gives the same result in a fresh process or after other episodes. The tests prove: test_new_stateful_agent_per_episode: one distinct agent per episode, each factory call has no arguments, and each agent sees its episode's steps exactly once from step 0. test_reuse_of_any_earlier_agent_is_rejected: A -> A, A -> B -> A and A -> B -> C -> B each stop the run at the reused agent, before it sees a step. test_distinct_agents_are_accepted: A -> B -> C is accepted, and agents that compare equal but are distinct objects run normally. test_resume_builds_agents_only_for_missing_episodes: after an interruption, resume builds agents only for the episodes that are not in the artifact, and the final artifact is byte-identical to an uninterrupted run. test_agent_receives_only_the_observation: under a distinctive 64-bit seed, every act call has exactly one positional argument of type Observation. Every object inside it is a known observation type. Its serialized form holds no seed (decimal or hex), manifest hash, suite hash or scenario hash. No observation object has a seed, rng_state, trapped, scenario or similar attribute. test_adapters_reproduce_plain_policy_artifacts: the always-stay, greedy and stateful counting adapters produce artifacts byte-identical to the plain function policies. The interface changes nothing in records or metrics. Limit: this is an interface contract for in-process Python code, not a sandbox (see evaluation.md section 4). An untrusted model must run behind an adapter that sends it only the serialized observation. 6. Failure semantics Every failure is fail-closed. Model output is never repaired, filtered, defaulted or retried by the interface. Failure Result missing ID for an active person ModelOutputError unknown ID ModelOutputError ID of an evacuated or casualty person ModelOutputError invalid action value ("up", None, 1, "NORTH") ModelOutputError action not in allowed_actions ModelOutputError malformed return value (not a mapping, non-string keys) ModelOutputError exception raised by the model the same exception object, unchanged factory returns a non-agent or any earlier agent EvaluationError step out of order for a bound agent EvaluationError ModelOutputError is a subclass of InvalidActionError. Its message is step <n>: followed by the simulator's own message, and its __cause__ is the simulator's InvalidActionError. Validation calls the simulator's parse_actions, so the interface and the simulator always accept and reject the same output (test_invalid_model_output_fails_closed checks both for every case). Any of these failures stops run_evaluation. The simulator is not stepped with the rejected output, and the artifact keeps only the episodes completed before the failure. A deterministic model under the same manifest gives the same failure and the same artifact bytes on every run. A failed episode is not recorded as a result: a model that fails must be fixed and the run resumed. 6.1 Timeouts The core has no timeout mechanism. The rule is: A provider or remote adapter enforces its own timeout inside act. On expiry it raises (for example TimeoutError). The exception propagates through Agent.act and run_evaluation unchanged. It is not wrapped, retried or converted into an action. The simulator is not stepped for that observation. The current episode is not committed to the artifact. The episodes completed before it stay in the artifact. A later run_evaluation call with resume=True runs only the missing episodes, each with a new agent. test_adapter_timeout_propagates_and_the_episode_is_not_committed checks each point, and that the resumed artifact is byte-identical to an uninterrupted run. 7. Optional execution accounting Accounting is evaluator-side and optional. Pass an observer: log: list[StepExecution] = [] factory = agent_policy_factory(MyAdapter, on_step=log.append) After each accepted act call the observer receives a StepExecution: Field Content step the observation step latency_seconds wall-clock time of the act call, measured by the evaluator reported ExecutionMetadata from the agent, or None An agent may implement last_execution() -> ExecutionMetadata | None (ReportsExecution). Every ExecutionMetadata field is optional and None means unknown: Field Content provider provider label model model label input_tokens input token count, a non-negative integer output_tokens output token count, a non-negative integer cost a finite non-negative number; needs cost_currency cost_currency currency code, for example "USD"; needs cost An adapter must report only what its provider returned. It must not estimate token counts or costs. Invalid values raise EvaluationError. Accounting never reaches the simulator, the run record, the metrics or the result artifact. It is read only when an observer is given, after the actions are validated. test_accounting_is_collected_but_never_changes_outcomes checks that an artifact with accounting is byte-identical to one without. Latency is not deterministic, so it must never be part of a canonical result. 8. Serialized observation serialize_observation(observation) returns the canonical JSON text of Observation.to_dict(): sorted keys, no whitespace, ASCII only, no NaN. This is the payload for a future external adapter. {"allowed_actions":["stay","north","south","east","west"],"burning":[[0,3]],"map":{"exits":[{"id":"E1","position":[0,4]}],"height":1,"obstacles":[],"width":5},"observation_version":"1.0","people":[{"id":"Pa","position":[0,0],"status":"active"}],"rules":{"conflict_resolution":"lowest_id_wins","enter_fire":"casualty","exits_flammable":true,"fire_model":"deterministic","max_steps":100,"spread_interval":1,"spread_probability":null},"step":0} Order is canonical: people and exits by ID, obstacles and burning cells by position (row, then column). The simulator produces observations in this order, so equal observations give equal bytes. deserialize_observation(text) parses the text back. It is strict: exactly the declared keys, the current observation_version, correct types, positions inside the grid, unique items in canonical order, and text that re-serializes to the same bytes. Anything else raises ObservationFormatError. observation_from_dict applies the same checks to a parsed object without the byte comparison. The tests prove that the serialized form: round-trips every observation of every public scenario under a greedy policy, has exactly the declared key set, with no seed, rng, hash, trapped, scenario, description, manifest, episode or index anywhere, holds no seed, RNG position, scenario hash or description, even for a stochastic scenario with a distinctive seed, is identical for two episodes that differ only in seed, scenario ID and description, does not change when a person is trapped. 9. Action payload serialize_actions(observation, output) returns the canonical external form of one step of model output, for a future external adapter: {"action_schema_version":"1.0","actions":{"Pa":"east","Pb":"stay"},"step":3} Key Content action_schema_version ACTION_SCHEMA_VERSION, currently "1.0" step the step of the observation the actions answer actions person ID -> action string, for exactly the active people The text is canonical JSON: sorted keys (so person IDs are sorted), no whitespace, ASCII only. The output is checked with validate_actions before it is serialized. deserialize_actions(observation, text) parses a payload for that observation and returns dict[str, Action]. It raises ModelOutputError (message step <n>: ...) unless all of these hold: the text is valid JSON with exactly the three keys above, action_schema_version is the supported version string, step is an integer equal to observation.step, actions is an object of string actions for exactly the active people, each in observation.allowed_actions, the text is byte-identical to its canonical form (no extra whitespace, other key order, duplicate keys or trailing newline). The payload holds no seed, RNG state, scenario data, accounting or other evaluator metadata. It is an exchange format only: run records and evaluation artifacts are unchanged and do not store it. 10. Versioning This interface wraps existing contracts and changes none of them. SIMULATOR_VERSION, OBSERVATION_VERSION, SCHEMA_VERSION, METRICS_VERSION, the evaluation manifest and result versions, and all scenario and suite hashes are unchanged (test_no_contract_version_changes). The two external formats are versioned independently: The serialized observation carries observation_version ("1.0"). A change to the observation fields must bump it, and old text is then rejected. The action payload carries action_schema_version (ACTION_SCHEMA_VERSION, "1.0"). A change to the payload must bump it, and old payloads are then rejected.

title: Published site data
description: How this site is generated and how to interpret API measurements.
text: Reading the published results The Anantam website presents official public development score reports from EMBERBench. The benchmark's simulation, scoring and model runners live in the benchmark repository; this website reads a generated result artifact. It does not present hidden-suite results. What is in this snapshot? The published snapshot contains 27 entries: 19 AI decision models and 8 hand-coded reference agents. The frozen schedule contains 19 worlds. Every published entry has one trial per world. These counts describe the current artifact, rather than a general promise about future evaluation releases. The run originally identified by jev-latest resolves to jev-1.13.0 and is displayed as typesafe/jev-1.13. Its original model ID remains intact for evidence links. The newer typesafe/jev-1.14 is a separate evaluated report. Results describe performance on the public diagnostic suite. They do not establish generalization to held-out environments, statistical superiority, or safety in real evacuations. Reading the charts The results page contains a ranking chart, a safety-versus-quality scatter plot, people outcomes, and a selected model's scenario scores. Selecting a model updates these views together. Scenario bars open the evaluated worlds with the same model selected. EMBER is a composite score from 0 to 100. It is not the percentage of people evacuated. Safety and Quality are 0–1 factors. The people-outcome chart uses recorded counts summed across evaluated worlds; these counts are not family-balanced scores. The default ranking follows the scoring specification. A custom metric sort changes the visual order without redefining official rank. Missing API measurements remain unavailable and are never plotted as zero. Reference agents are hand-coded programs, rather than another group of commercial AI models. For definitions, read EMBER scoring, Episode metrics, and Statistical analysis. API cost and latency API measurements come from the run metadata. Some costs are provider-reported; others are estimates derived from token counts and recorded list prices. The website marks estimates with ≈. These are measurements of the evaluated runs, not live pricing quotations. Mean decision latency measures the recorded wait for one action call. It is different from total run wall time, which can include rate-limit waits and other overhead. If a run was resumed, API metadata may describe only its final invocation. Requests and token counts should be interpreted with that coverage limit in mind. Cost, tokens, request counts and latency never change the EMBER Score. An absent measurement does not mean the model used no resources. Confidence intervals The displayed 95% intervals come from the score report's stratified resampling procedure. With one published trial per model, these intervals cannot measure unobserved between-trial variability. Visual score differences do not establish a statistically significant winner. The separate comparison page shows descriptive differences. Official paired inference requires matching scoring versions, constants, manifests, packs and applicable episodes. Those official comparison outputs are not part of the website's data artifact. Trace a result Model profiles retain the evaluated model ID, trials and result digests. Scenario evidence retains the scenario and model context. The methodology page exposes the suite, EnvironmentPack, pack digest and scoring version for this snapshot. The artifact contains no evaluation timestamp. A page load time, file modification time or model order must not be interpreted as a “last evaluated” date. You can read the generated results artifact directly, or inspect integrity and provenance and frozen environments for the underlying verification rules. How results are published The data builder reads finished run directories containing official score reports and optional API summaries. It validates that the reports belong to the same frozen pack and scoring version, then writes site/data/results.js. That file is generated; displayed values must never be entered by hand in interface code. Documentation is hosted as static pages on this site and works independently of loading the result artifact. The benchmark guides are mirrored from a recorded source revision, with their original Markdown available for download and the Apache License 2.0 preserved.

title: EMBER scoring
description: The complete score definition, aggregation and ranking rules.
text: The EMBER Score (scoring version 1.0) This document is the normative definition of the EMBER Score. The code is src/emberbench/scoring.py. The tests are tests/test_scoring.py. The research, the candidate formulas and the sensitivity study that justify each choice are in benchmark-methodology.md. The frozen environment that every model is scored on is in environment-pack.md. The EMBER Score is one number in [0, 100]. Its unit is benchmark-performance points under EMBER scoring version 1.0. It is not a percentage of people evacuated. A report says "72.4 points under EMBER scoring version 1.0", never "72.4% evacuated". 1. Status and versioning Item Value Version SCORING_VERSION = "1.0" Constants OFFICIAL_CONSTANTS (section 4); ScoringConstants.digest() pins them Separate from simulator, observation, action schema, scenario schema, metrics, crowd diagnostics, statistics, generator and evaluation versions. Scoring changes none of them. Provenance benchmark_versions()["scoring"]; benchmark revision 2 and later pin it (see integrity.md section 12) SCORING_VERSION changes when a definition, a constant, the arithmetic or the serialization changes. A score is comparable with another score only when both have the same scoring version, the same constants digest, the same evaluation manifest and the same environment pack. A score is official only when it is computed against an environment pack whose evaluation manifest equals the results' manifest, under OFFICIAL_CONSTANTS. ScoreReport.official tells which. A score against a bare suite is labelled UNOFFICIAL. 2. Inputs and authentication score_results(trials, target, *, failures=None, resamples=2000) takes: trials: one or more EvaluationResult objects of the same model on the same evaluation manifest. Use one trial for a deterministic policy and several for a stochastic model (section 12). target: the Suite, or the EnvironmentPack. failures[t]: an optional map from episode index to FailureKind that says why trial t has no result for a scheduled episode. Every result is authenticated from scratch, exactly as in statistics.md: the manifest must round-trip and target the suite, every run record is replayed (verify_record), and the stored metrics must equal the recomputed metrics. With a pack, every scheduled episode's fire trajectory must also match the pack's fire_world_digest, and every recorded burning set must match that trajectory. Any difference raises ScoringInputError. There is no partial score. Provider-reported success, accuracy or cost is never an input. Scoring is local and uses only replayed records. 3. Privileged references Several components compare the model with a relaxed single-person optimum. The optimum is computed by backward induction over (cell, step) for one person alone who knows the whole future fire and follows the simulator phase order. Other people can only block moves, so each reference is a lower bound for every policy. The references use the evaluator seed. They are evaluator-side only, like emberbench.oracle, and never reach a model. For each scheduled episode and each person i at start cell x_i: Reference Definition M* (max_evacuated) number of people with a finite earliest evacuation step. Equal to privileged_escape_bound(...).earliest_evacuation (tested on every public scenario). L_i earliest evacuation step from (x_i, 0) m*_i fewest cell moves of any escape from (x_i, 0) (the move onto the exit counts) D*_i fewest danger-zone person-states of any escape from (x_i, 0) L(x, t) earliest evacuation step from cell x at snapshot t A person-state is in the danger zone when the Manhattan distance d from the person's cell to the nearest burning cell satisfies 0 < d <= 2 (HAZARD_RADIUS = 2). The distance ignores walls, like the metrics exposure proxy. The transition rule is the simulator's: from (x, t) a person may stay or move to an open neighbour y, unless y burns at the start of the step; a non-burning exit evacuates at once; any other y must not burn after the fire phase. Snapshot H (max_steps) has no successor. 4. The episode score For one authenticated episode with M* >= 1: EMBER = 100 * Safety * Quality ^ beta * Severity Safety = E * P_casualty * P_stranding (0 at the catastrophic gate) Quality = weighted geometric mean of the defined quality components beta = min(1, ln(alpha_c) / ln(q_min)) = ln 0.6 / ln 0.5 = 0.7369655941662... Severity = product over severe components k of phi * (q_k / q_k_severe) ^ gamma Every component, Safety, Quality and Severity are in [0, 1]. No component can exceed 1, so no strength offsets a failure. Safety caps the score (section 5), and each severe quality failure caps it again (section 4.3). Trajectory invariance (a V1 invariant). Every score input is a function of the authenticated state trajectory: positions, statuses and the fire, step by step. No input comes from the action log alone. So two runs with byte-identical state trajectories get identical scores, whatever actions produced them. test_block_scrub_keeps_trajectory_and_score checks this on replayed public episodes (section 4.2). 4.1 Safety and person-level attribution Every loss is attributed per person. A person i is savable when the privileged earliest escape L_i (section 3) is finite. Then, for every person at the end of the episode: Outcome Savable Not savable evacuated evacuated evacuated (cannot happen: L_i would be finite) died avoidable casualty unavoidable casualty still active or stranded at the horizon avoidable stranded unavoidable stranded c and s are the numbers of avoidable casualties and avoidable stranded people. The evidence stores the sorted person IDs of all four loss classes (avoidable_casualty_ids, avoidable_stranded_ids, unavoidable_casualty_ids, unavoidable_stranded_ids), so each count can be audited person by person. An unavoidable loss is never transferred between people. An earlier draft computed c = max(0, C - U) with U = N - M* from aggregate counts. That rule lets the unavoidable loss of one person hide the avoidable death of another: with person a savable but dead and person b unsavable and stranded, the draft gives c = 0, but the correct value is c = 1. test_real_episode_person_level_attribution reproduces this case with a real replayed episode. The evidence validator rejects any record where the identity sets overlap, are not sorted, or do not match the counts. Factor Formula Official constants Evacuation E (evacuated / M*) ^ kE kE = 2 Casualty P_casualty alpha_c ^ log2(1 + c) * (1 - c / M*) ^ k_c alpha_c = 0.6, k_c = 4 Stranding P_stranding alpha_s ^ log2(1 + s) * (1 - s / M*) ^ k_s alpha_s = 0.8, k_s = 2 Catastrophic gate Safety = 0 when (c + s) / M* >= 1/2 catastrophic_loss_rate = 1/2 The incident factor alpha ^ log2(1 + n) is paid in full for the first loss and again for every doubling of 1 + n. It makes the first casualty expensive in any population. The rate term (1 - n / M*) ^ k grows with the share of people lost. A casualty costs more than a stranded person. Stranding and incomplete evacuation are penalized independently of casualties. 4.2 Quality components Component Formula Defined when Weight Time T Q_cut / sum(A_i) over evacuees; A_i is the evacuation step, Q_cut the capacity bound (below) at least one evacuee 3/8 Hazard H (1 - (D - D*) / sum(A_i)) ^ kH over evacuees; D = their danger-zone states, D* = sum(D*_i) at least one evacuee 2/8 Path P sum(m*_i) / sum(m_i) over evacuees; m_i = cells moved at least one evacuee 1/8 Replanning R sum(L(x_e, t_e) - t_e) / sum(r_e - t_e) over recoverable route-invalidation events at least one recoverable event 2/8 Constant: kH = 1. There is no Coordination component (see "Congestion is not a score input" below). Every ratio is a privileged lower bound over the actual value, so it is in (0, 1]. If an actual value is below its bound, the record is rejected: that can only happen with a forged record. Time capacity bound Q_cut. The sum of single-person optimum steps sum(L_i) ignores that people queue. Q_cut adds the two capacity limits that no policy can avoid. Both are lower bounds on sum(A_i) for every policy, and sum(L_i) <= Q_exit <= Q_cut <= sum(A_i): Exit capacity (Q_exit, evacuee_time_queue_bound). Positions after movement are distinct, so in each step at most one person leaves through each exit cell that is not burning at the start of the step. Q_exit is the list schedule of the evacuees' release steps L_i over these exit slots. For unit jobs with release dates, the list schedule minimizes the sum of finish steps. Cut capacity (Q_cut, evacuee_time_cut_bound, the Time reference). Let w be the wall-only distance to the nearest exit. For a threshold d >= 1, take a connected component K of the open cells with w > d. A move changes w by at most 1 and exits have w = 0, so every escape from K first steps onto N(K), the cells next to K with w = d: a vertex cut, for example a door. Positions are distinct, so in step s at most k_s people stand on N(K), where k_s counts the cut cells that burn neither at the start nor at the end of the step. An evacuee i that starts in K first enters the cut in a step s_i >= r_i, its earliest single-person arrival on a cut cell from which escape is still possible, and needs at least q_i more steps from there (the least single-person remaining time over the cut cells and snapshots it can reach). So A_i >= s_i + q_i and A_i >= L_i. The list schedule of the entries minimizes sum(s_i). Components whose cuts share cells are merged, so each person is in at most one group; people outside every group add L_i. Q_cut is the maximum over all thresholds and Q_exit. Every step of the derivation is a relaxation, so Q_cut is a lower bound for every policy (proof in _cut_bound, validated on every episode of the study: section 6 of benchmark-methodology.md). A queue that no policy can avoid, at an exit or at a door, is therefore not charged to Time. A queue that a policy causes, for example by sending everyone to one exit when a second exit is free, is charged (test_real_episode_unavoidable_door_queue_is_not_charged, test_real_episode_avoidable_queue_is_charged). Congestion is not a score input. Version 1.0 at commit ce5e322 had a Coordination component (1 - block rate)^2 and a severe gate at a block rate above 1/4. It was removed, because a blocked move is an action-log event, not a trajectory event: The scrub proof. Under the public movement resolver, a person whose move is blocked by another person (occupied, conflict or cycle) stays in place. If that move is replaced by STAY, the person still stays in place. Every other person's resulting cell is unchanged too: a blocked person never vacates its cell and never takes a target cell, so no successful move depends on it, and every move that was blocked behind it is itself scrubbed. So replacing every congestion-blocked move with STAY gives the identical state trajectory with zero blocks. The resolver is public and pure and its inputs are all in the observation, so any agent can do this. The adversary adv-block-scrub does it to congestion-aware-v1: identical state trajectories in every study episode, and a gain of several points under the old score (section 6 of benchmark-methodology.md). No lower bound. The block count has no positive privileged lower bound: the scrub reaches 0 for every trajectory. A ratio "bound / actual" like the other components cannot exist. Not a skill. A policy that predicts the resolver's tie-breaks and emits STAY instead of a blocked move evacuates the same people at the same steps on the same cells. It is not a better evacuation policy, so the difference must not be scored. The realized cost is already scored. A bottleneck costs delay (Time, against Q_cut), exposure while waiting (Hazard) and, at worst, lives (Safety). Every trajectory-only congestion measure tried (waiting steps above the capacity-forced delay, excess person-time over Q_cut) is a function of the Time and Path inputs, so it would count the same delay twice. Dead people are not charged twice. The blocked moves of people who later die were part of the old block rate, and their deaths are in Safety. Time, Path and Hazard are over evacuees only, and blocks are not an input, so no loss is charged twice. Congestion stays mandatory in every report as diagnostics (ScoreReport.diagnostics, CongestionDiagnostics): congestion block rate, contested cell-steps, hotspot cells, peak contested cells and exit throughput (evacuations per exit-step inside each exit's active window). They explain a score; they never change it (test_congestion_blocks_are_diagnostics_not_score_inputs). Exit utilization is diagnostic only. A balanced split between exits is not a goal: the right split depends on distances, fire and capacity. The capacity bound already measures the only effect of exit allocation that the score needs, the time cost of a bad allocation, against an allocation-optimal bound. A separate balance or allocation-regret term would count that cost twice. Route-invalidation event. At step t >= 1 the burning set changed and, for a person active in snapshot t, the fire-aware distance to the nearest non-burning exit (shortest path through non-wall, non-burning cells) became longer or infinite, where it was finite before. The event is recoverable when L(x_e, t) is finite. Its resolution step r_e is the person's evacuation step, or the horizon H when the person is lost (censored). An unrecoverable event is counted but not scored: its outcome is already in Safety. Quality is the weighted geometric mean over the defined components, with the weights renormalized over them: Quality = exp( sum_k (w_k / W) * ln q_k ), W = sum of the weights of the defined components Quality = 0 when any defined component is 0 An undefined component is never set to 1. It is left out, and its weight is shared by the others. So an episode without route invalidation is neither rewarded nor punished for replanning. Path uses the fire-aware privileged bound m*_i, so a detour that the fire makes necessary is not charged. Hazard is measured above the privileged minimum D*, so exposure that no policy can avoid is not charged. Neither component counts the same loss as Safety: both are computed over evacuees only. 4.3 Quality exponent and severe failures Two rules make Safety dominate without making Quality irrelevant. Quality exponent beta. Quality enters as Quality ^ beta, with beta = min(1, ln(alpha_c) / ln(q_min)), q_min = smallest severe threshold in component space beta is derived, not tuned. With every quality component at or above its severe threshold, Quality >= q_min, so Quality ^ beta >= alpha_c = 0.6. A perfect run with one avoidable casualty has Safety < 0.6. So a run with no avoidable loss and no severe failure always scores above a perfect run with one avoidable casualty, in every population (requirement R12, tested for M* from 2 to 1000, also with one extra stranded person on both sides). Severe failures. A quality component is severe when it crosses a threshold in natural units. The comparison is exact and strict: Component Severe when Threshold in component space q_k_severe Time T < 1/2 (more than twice the capacity bound Q_cut) 0.5 Hazard avoidable danger-zone rate > 1/4 1 - 1/4 = 0.75 Path P < 1/2 (more than twice the fewest cells) 0.5 Replanning R < 1/2 0.5 Each severe component k multiplies the score by phi * (q_k / q_k_severe) ^ gamma, with phi = 0.8 and gamma = 1. So one severe failure caps the episode below 80, and the cap falls further as the failure gets worse. Two severe failures cap it below 64. Severity is a ceiling, not a separate measurement: it applies to the same components that are already in Quality, and is 1 when nothing is severe. The report counts severe episode-trials per component (Robustness.severe_episode_trials). The episode record gives severity, the list severe and the ceiling = 100 * Safety * Severity. The thresholds are set by normative requirements, not by a policy ranking (see benchmark-methodology.md, section 6): evacuating more than twice as slowly as the capacity optimum, one avoidable danger-zone step in four, twice the needed cells and twice the needed recovery time are each a failure of that dimension. A severe bottleneck is a severe Time failure: it is measured by the delay it causes, not by blocked actions. Mild congestion that the capacity bound explains never triggers a gate. 4.4 Episode statuses Status Meaning Score scored authenticated, below the gate 100 * Safety * Quality ^ beta * Severity catastrophic authenticated, avoidable loss rate >= 1/2 0 failed scheduled, no authenticated result 0 not_applicable M* = 0: no policy can save anyone excluded from every mean, for every model A failed episode has a FailureKind: missing (no declared reason), invalid_output (ModelOutputError or another rejected action set), model_error (the model or its adapter raised) or timeout (the adapter's deadline expired). All four score 0 and are counted in the report. A failure can never disappear: a gap without a declaration is missing. A declaration for an unscheduled episode, or for an episode that has a committed result, is rejected. not_applicable depends only on the scenario and the seed, never on the model. 4.5 Arithmetic Counts and references are exact integers. Non-integer powers are computed with Python decimal (libmpdec) at 50 significant digits, round-half-even, which gives identical digits on every platform. Components are rounded to 1e-12 and the episode score to 1e-9 points. From there on every mean and every bootstrap statistic is exact rational arithmetic. 5. Exact penalties and ceilings Single-failure profile under the official constants. Everything else is perfect; replanning is undefined. Case (population 100 unless stated) Score perfect 100.0 1 avoidable casualty 56.5 2 casualties 39.4 3 casualties 30.0 5 casualties 19.6 10 casualties 9.1 25 casualties 1.6 1 casualty in a population of 4 10.7 1 stranded 76.8 10 stranded 30.3 1 savable casualty + 1 unsavable stranded person 56.5 50 losses (the gate) 0.0 Time 0.9 / 0.8 / 0.5 (threshold) 96.2 / 92.1 / 77.5 Time 0.4 / 0.25 / 0.1 (severe) 45.7 / 24.0 / 6.8 any block rate, no delay (blocks are diagnostics) 100.0 avoidable danger-zone rate 0.1 / 0.3 (severe) 97.4 / 68.4 Path 0.6 / 0.4 (severe) 93.9 / 57.2 Replanning 0.8 / 0.3 (severe), replanning defined 96.0 / 38.5 every quality component exactly at its threshold 64.7 Time is relative to the capacity bound Q_cut, so "Time 0.5" is a realized bottleneck that doubles the evacuees' person-time over the best that any policy could do. The jump at a threshold is the severe factor phi = 0.8 times the ratio q / q_severe. Below the thresholds, Quality still matters: Time 0.5 alone costs 22.5 points. Ceilings that follow from the formula: Any avoidable casualty: the episode score is at most 100 * 0.6 = 60, for every population size. Any avoidable stranded person: at most 100 * 0.8 * (1 - 1/M*)^4 < 80. No 95 or more after a meaningful safety failure: any avoidable casualty or stranded person gives a score below 80. A casualty is worse than a stranding: one avoidable casualty scores below one avoidable stranded person in the same episode. Any severe quality failure: below 100 * 0.8 = 80; two severe failures, below 64. A severe failure cannot be bought back by any other component, because no component exceeds 1. Catastrophic failure: half or more of the people who could be saved are lost: 0. Invalid output, model error, missing result: 0. Timeout: 0, the most severe penalty. 6. Aggregation Episodes are aggregated in a fixed hierarchy. Each level is the unweighted mean of the defined values of the level below: episode-trial -> episode (mean over trials) episode -> scenario (mean over its applicable seeds) scenario -> primary family (mean over its scenarios) family -> overall (mean over families) = the EMBER Score The primary family is SuiteEntry.primary_family. A scenario counts in one family only, so a scenario with several families is not counted twice. A scenario whose episodes are all not_applicable is excluded. The report also gives the scenario-balanced mean (mean of scenario means) and the micro mean (mean of all episodes). They are diagnostics. The family-balanced mean is the headline: each failure mode weighs the same, and a suite cannot raise a score by adding easy scenarios of one family. Components, Safety and Quality are aggregated with the same hierarchy over the episode-trials where they are defined. Each component reports its coverage defined / total. Lower tail. The report gives the median scenario score, the worst scenario and its ID, the type-7 10th percentile of episode scores, CVaR10 (the mean of the lowest ceil(n/10) episode scores), and the number of zero-score episode-trials by cause (catastrophic and each FailureKind). Totals. Escapable, evacuated, avoidable casualties, avoidable stranded and unavoidable losses, summed over scored episode-trials, also per trial. 7. Confidence interval The 95% interval of the headline is a stratified two-stage percentile bootstrap: Strata are the primary families. In each resample, inside each family, draw as many scenarios as it has, with replacement; inside each drawn scenario, draw as many episodes as it has, with replacement. Recompute the family-balanced mean. Bounds are the type-7 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles of resamples (default 2000) statistics. The random stream is the SHAKE-256 counter-mode BootstrapStream of statistics.md, seeded with SHA-256 of the canonical JSON of the scoring version, the constants digest, the manifest hash, the model ID and the exact episode scores. The interval is identical on every platform. With fewer than 5 applicable episodes there is no interval. The interval describes this evaluation sample: these scenarios and these seeds. When a family has one scenario, the bootstrap cannot see scenario variance, and a deterministic model on deterministic scenarios gets a zero-width interval. To make claims about unseen environments, use a generated suite with several scenarios per family (see procedural-generation.md). 8. Comparison and leaderboard compare_scores(a, b) pairs two reports episode by episode. The reports must have the same scoring version, constants, manifest, pack and applicable episodes. Paired differences d_e = a_e - b_e are aggregated with the same hierarchy (so delta = score_a - score_b exactly), and the interval is the same stratified bootstrap applied to the differences. The outcome is one of four: Outcome Rule exact_tie every paired episode score is identical a_better interval lower bound > 0 and delta >= 1.0 point b_better interval upper bound < 0 and -delta >= 1.0 point inconclusive anything else, including fewer than 5 applicable episodes practical_difference = 1 point is the smallest difference that counts as "better". A difference that is statistically clear but smaller is inconclusive. Leaderboard order is separate from significance. leaderboard_order sorts by: the score rounded half-even to 0.1 point, descending; the Safety factor, descending; avoidable casualties per trial, ascending; avoidable stranded per trial, ascending; the worst scenario score, descending; the model ID. So safety decides every tie of the displayed score. Adjacent leaderboard entries can still be inconclusive; publish the comparison next to the order. 9. Metric classification Every existing metric of metrics.md has one role: Metric Role Use in the score evacuated / evacuation rate core (Safety) E, relative to M* casualties (fatality) safety gate and core (Safety) P_casualty on avoidable (savable) casualties, catastrophic gate stranded safety gate and core (Safety) P_stranding on avoidable stranded people, catastrophic gate time to safety (time.*) core (Quality) and severe gate T, evacuees only, relative to the capacity bound Q_cut; a realized bottleneck is charged here congestion / bottleneck (blocked_*, congestion_block_rate) diagnostic only, mandatory in every report none; an action-log count (section 4.2) fire exposure (fire_exposure, min_fire_distance) diagnostic replaced by the avoidable danger-zone rate H (core and severe gate) path efficiency (path_efficiency.*, static bound) diagnostic replaced by P with the fire-aware privileged bound (core, low weight, severe gate) replanning proxies (recovery_proxy_rate and others) diagnostic replaced by R on route-invalidation events (core and severe gate) exit utilization / balance diagnostic only none; a 50/50 split is never rewarded; the time cost of a bad allocation is in T through Q_cut crowd diagnostics (hotspots, contested cells, exit throughput) diagnostic only, mandatory in every report none decisions, latency, input/output tokens, cost, retries, timeouts operational only none; OperationalRecord, see section 11 Reasons for each role are in benchmark-methodology.md, section 4. 10.
