Interpretation: what 70/100 means 70.0/100 is 70.0 benchmark-performance points under SCORING_VERSION 1.0. It is not "70% of people evacuated". An episode with any avoidable casualty scores below 60. So an episode score of 70 means nobody who could be saved died. An episode with a severe quality failure scores below 80. So an episode score of 80 or more means no avoidable loss and no severe failure. The headline is a mean over families. 70 can be "every family safe with moderate quality" or "seven families perfect and three at zero". The family scores and the lower-tail statistics tell which. Always read them with the headline. Anchors on the public suite with the development seeds 0, 1, 2: congestion-aware-v1 53.2, fire-aware-shortest-path-v1 40.4, static-shortest-path-v1 37.4, nearest-exit-greedy-v1 27.5, random-legal-v1 0.0, always-stay 0.0. The privileged bound would score 100 but is not a policy. A report has this shape (format_summary(report), family list shortened): EMBER Score 53.2 / 100 benchmark-performance points under EMBER scoring version 1.0 95% CI [50.6, 58.5] (stratified two-stage bootstrap, 2000 resamples; this sample only) Model congestion-aware-v1; trials 1; official; environment pack <id> sha256:<digest> Safety factor 0.556; quality factor 0.929 Components (0-1, defined/total): evacuation 0.864 (30/30); casualty 0.590 (30/30); stranding 1.000 (30/30); time 0.936 (30/30); hazard 0.896 (30/30); path 0.932 (30/30); replanning 1.000 (8/30) Primary families: single_exit_low_density 99.1; single_exit_high_density 31.2; narrow_corridor_bottleneck 95.5; ... Tail: median scenario 37.7; worst scenario 7.4 (v1-pub-05-central-ignition); p10 episode 16.0; CVaR10 7.4 Zero-score episode-trials 0 of 30: catastrophic 0; missing 0; invalid_output 0; model_error 0; timeout 0 Severe quality failures (episode-trials): time 0; hazard 3; path 0; replanning 0 People per trial: escapable 561.0; evacuated 526.0; avoidable casualties 35.0; avoidable stranded 0.0 Congestion diagnostics (not scored): block rate 0.399; contested cell-steps per trial 1707.0; hotspot cells per trial 447.0; peak contested cells 20; exit throughput 0.776 The EMBER Score is not a percentage of people evacuated. 11. Operational metrics and EMBER-Efficiency Tokens, money and latency are never inputs to the score. score_results has no parameter for them. Record them in an OperationalRecord, next to the score: Field Meaning model_id, provider_id the exact model snapshot and the provider inference_config_digest inference_config_digest(config): SHA-256 of the canonical JSON of every inference setting (temperature, top-p, max tokens, seed if any, system prompt version, adapter version) trials, episodes the work the record covers latency_seconds evaluator-measured wall time input_tokens, output_tokens kept separate, never summed cost, cost_unit evaluator-computed cost (exact fraction) and its unit; None when unknown retries, timeouts adapter retries and expired deadlines The record is validated (no empty IDs, a 64-hex digest, non-negative finite values) and has its own digest. efficiency_view(report, cost_per_episode, unit) gives an optional EMBER-Efficiency view: points per unit of evaluator-measured cost. It does not change the score or the order. 12. Model stochasticity A deterministic policy needs one trial. A model that can give different actions for the same observation (any sampled LLM) needs K >= 3 repeated trials on the same pack, with pinned inference settings (one inference_config_digest). temperature = 0 is not a guarantee of determinism: batching, kernel choice and provider changes can alter outputs. Every trial is scored; the best trial is never selected. Each episode's trials are averaged before aggregation, so trials never count as extra scenarios. The protocol is in environment-pack.md, section 6. 13. Relation to the metrics rules metrics.md, section 11, requires a composite to be versioned, decomposable, and to never let speed buy safety. Version 1.0 meets all three: It has its own version and constants digest, and every report holds the components, the severe-failure list and the per-person evidence. Within one episode, a run with no avoidable loss and no severe quality failure always scores above a perfect run with one avoidable casualty (section 4.3). Speed can only help a run with a casualty against a safe run that itself fails a dimension severely, for example one that evacuates more than twice as slowly as the capacity bound. Such a run is not "safe and good"; the severe gate makes that explicit. Leaderboard ties of the displayed score are always broken by safety first (section 8).

title: Episode metrics
description: Raw outcomes, timing, paths and authenticated measurements.
text: Per-episode metrics (metrics version 1.0) This document defines every field returned by emberbench.compute_episode_metrics(scenario, record) -> EpisodeMetrics. The code is in src/emberbench/metrics.py. The exact-value tests are in tests/test_metrics.py. The metrics describe one episode: one scenario, one seed, one action log. Aggregation across seeds or scenarios, robustness statistics and leaderboards are out of scope here (see Issue #12). 1. Principles Raw metrics are canonical. Every field is a count, a step number, a cell distance or a ratio of named counts. Each ratio states its numerator and denominator. No composite score in the metrics. The metrics have no single score and METRICS_VERSION does not change. The EMBER Score is a separate, separately versioned layer on top of these metrics: see scoring.md and section 11. Safety first. Speed fields that only cover evacuees always come with the counts of people who did not evacuate. The person-time-to-safety metric counts every person. Proxies are named as proxies. The fire-exposure and replanning fields describe observable events. They do not measure risk or model intent. Fail closed. Inputs that do not belong together, a malformed record, or a record that the simulator could not have produced raise MetricsInputError. No partial result is returned. Exact arithmetic. Every ratio is computed as an exact fractions.Fraction and converted to float once. A value is the correctly rounded float of an exact rational, on every platform. Pure function. The scenario and the record are not mutated. METRICS_VERSION changes whenever a definition in this document changes. 2. Inputs and validation Source Used for Scenario population and person IDs, initial positions, walls, grid size, exit IDs and positions, termination.max_steps RunRecord header versions, scenario_id, scenario_hash, seed RunRecord.initial_state snapshot s_0 (positions and initial burning cells) RunRecord.steps[t] actions, movement outcomes, ignitions, evacuations, casualties and snapshot s_t RunRecord.final_state terminal status of each person, terminal trapped set, termination reason compute_episode_metrics validates its inputs in three stages, in this order. All stages always run; there is no option to skip one. It raises MetricsInputError when any check fails. Stage 1 and 2: compatibility and structural validation. Compatibility. simulator_version equals SIMULATOR_VERSION, observation_version equals OBSERVATION_VERSION, and schema_version is supported and equals the scenario's. scenario_id equals the scenario's. scenario_hash equals scenario.content_hash(). Initial state. Step 0, every scenario person active at the scenario position, burning cells equal to the ignitions, not terminated, and a trapped set equal to a recomputation. Each step t. Step numbers are 1, 2, ..., T. Actions and movements cover exactly the people active in s_{t-1}. Each movement agrees with its action, origin and outcome; a moved target is in bounds and not a wall; no two people end in one cell. Ignitions are new, non-wall cells, and burning(s_t) = burning(s_{t-1}) ∪ ignited_t. Every evacuation and casualty event matches one status change (with the correct exit ID and casualty cause), resolved people never change, no active person stands on a burning cell or a usable exit, and the trapped set equals a recomputation. Termination. Only the last snapshot is terminated. Its reason is all_resolved when nobody is active, otherwise max_steps when T = max_steps. A record with no steps, or one that does not reach termination, is rejected: metrics need a complete episode. These checks give precise diagnostics and confirm every assumption the metrics rely on. On their own they only prove internal consistency. Stage 3: simulator replay authentication. compute_episode_metrics then calls verify_record(scenario, record). It replays the recorded action log from the recorded seed and requires a byte-identical record. A ReplayMismatchError becomes a MetricsInputError whose message starts with record failed simulator replay verification:; the original error is kept as __cause__. This stage rejects records that pass every structural check but are impossible under the simulator, for example a blocked_wall outcome for a move into an open cell, or an ignition that the configured fire model and RNG stream would not produce. Callers do not need to call verify_record themselves. 3. Notation N = population = number of people in the scenario (always >= 1). T = episode_steps = number of recorded steps. H = scenario.termination.max_steps (the horizon). s_0 = initial snapshot; s_t = snapshot after step t, for t = 1..T. A(s) = people with status active in snapshot s. A decision is one movement record: one active person at one step. The number of decisions is D = Σ_{t=1..T} |A(s_{t-1})|. ratio(a, b) = a / b, or null (None) when b = 0. 4. Safety (safety) Field Definition Unit population N people evacuated people with terminal status evacuated people casualties people with terminal status casualty people stranded people still active at termination people evacuated_rate evacuated / N fraction casualty_rate casualties / N fraction stranded_rate stranded / N fraction terminal_trapped_count ` final_state.trapped terminal_trapped_rate terminal_trapped_count / N fraction casualties_by_cause casualties per CasualtyCause (entered_fire, fire_spread) people Invariants: evacuated + casualties + stranded = N exactly (checked; a mismatch raises), and terminal_trapped_count <= stranded. When the episode ends with all_resolved, stranded = 0 and the trapped set is empty. 5. Time (time) Field Definition Unit episode_steps T steps max_steps H (from the scenario) steps evacuees E = number of evacuated people people non_evacuees N - E (casualties and stranded) people evacuation_steps for each evacuee, the step t whose evacuations list names it; sorted by person ID steps first_evacuation_step min of evacuation_steps; null if E = 0 step last_evacuation_step max of evacuation_steps; null if E = 0 step mean_evacuation_step ratio(Σ evacuation_steps, E) steps median_evacuation_step middle value; for even E, the mean of the two middle values; null if E = 0 steps person_time_to_safety_total Σ_i τ_i (see below) person-steps mean_person_time_to_safety person_time_to_safety_total / N steps Person-time-to-safety. For each person i: τ_i = evacuation step of i if i evacuated τ_i = H otherwise (casualty or stranded) Non-evacuees are censored at the horizon H. Every evacuation step is <= H, so a casualty or a stranded person can never look faster than any evacuee. The sum covers all N people, so this metric cannot hide a casualty. The censoring value is the scenario horizon, not T: an episode that ends early because the last people died does not get a smaller value. mean_evacuation_step and median_evacuation_step are evacuee-only statistics. They always come with evacuees and non_evacuees, and a run must never be compared on them alone. A run that loses its slowest people gets a lower evacuee mean. 6. Movement and congestion (movement) Each decision has exactly one MoveOutcome: stayed, moved, or one of the six blocked_* outcomes. Field Definition Denominator decisions D — stay_actions decisions with action stay (outcome stayed) — movement_attempts D - stay_actions (action is a direction) — successful_moves outcome moved — blocked_moves outcome blocked_* — blocked_by_outcome count per blocked outcome: boundary, wall, fire, occupied, conflict, cycle — congestion_blocks blocked_occupied + blocked_conflict + blocked_cycle (blocks caused by other people) — stay_rate ratio(stay_actions, decisions) decisions blocked_rate ratio(blocked_moves, movement_attempts) movement attempts congestion_block_rate ratio(congestion_blocks, movement_attempts) movement attempts Invariant: successful_moves + blocked_moves = movement_attempts (checked). Under enter_fire: casualty, a move into fire is moved; the person then becomes a casualty in the same step. 7. Path efficiency (path_efficiency and per person) For each person i: cells_moved_i = number of the person's decisions with outcome moved. Each such move changes the cell by exactly one 4-neighbour step. static_exit_distance_i = L_i = length of the shortest 4-neighbour path from the initial cell to any exit, through any non-wall cell in the grid. It ignores all fire (including the initial ignitions) and all people. It is null when no exit can be reached around the walls. L_i uses only the scenario geometry. It is a static lower bound: it is not a dynamically feasible path and not an oracle-optimal dynamic path. Under spreading fire and congestion, the best achievable path can be longer. For each evacuee (L_i is always defined and >= 1, and cells_moved_i >= L_i; a violation raises): path_efficiency_i = L_i / cells_moved_i in (0, 1] detour_ratio_i = cells_moved_i / L_i in [1, ∞) Both are null for casualties and stranded people. Episode aggregates, over the M evacuees: Field Definition evacuees_measured M total_cells_moved Σ cells_moved_i total_static_lower_bound Σ L_i aggregate_path_efficiency ratio(Σ L_i, Σ cells_moved_i) (ratio of sums) mean_path_efficiency ratio(Σ path_efficiency_i, M) mean_detour_ratio ratio(Σ detour_ratio_i, M) Path efficiency measures distance, not time. A blocked or stay step costs time but no distance. 8. Fire-exposure proxy (fire_exposure and per person) This is a deterministic proximity proxy, not a physical model of heat or smoke. It has no tuned constants. The person-states are all pairs (t, i) with t = 0..T and i ∈ A(s_t): every active person in every recorded snapshot, including s_0 and the terminal snapshot. Let B_t = burning(s_t). For each person-state with B_t ≠ ∅: d(t, i) = min_{f ∈ B_t} ( |row_i - row_f| + |col_i - col_f| ) This is the Manhattan distance on the grid. It ignores walls: a wall does not shield a person in this proxy. An active person is never on a burning cell in a snapshot, so d >= 1. The exposure is: exposure_total = Σ_{(t, i) : B_t ≠ ∅} 1 / d(t, i) mean_exposure = exposure_total / active_person_states Field Definition active_person_states `Σ_{t=0..T} person_states_with_fire person-states with B_t ≠ ∅ person_states_without_fire person-states with B_t = ∅ (they add 0) distance_histogram (d, count) for each observed d, sorted by d adjacent_person_states count with d = 1 min_fire_distance smallest observed d; null if no fire was ever present with someone active exposure_total as above (unit: person-states weighted by 1/d) mean_exposure as above Per person: min_fire_distance and fire_exposure (the same sum, limited to that person's states). Recomputing alternatives. distance_histogram and person_states_without_fire are the raw components. Any proxy of the form Σ g(d) can be recomputed from them, for example a threshold count (Σ_{d <= k} count) or another decay. exposure_total equals Σ count / d over the histogram. Limitation. People who leave the grid stop accumulating exposure. A casualty therefore can have a low exposure. Always read the proxy together with the safety counts. 9. Exit utilization (exits) Let n_e be the number of evacuations through exit e, E = Σ n_e, and K the number of exits in the scenario. Field Definition exit_count K exits_used number of exits with n_e >= 1 evacuations_per_exit (exit_id, n_e) for every exit, sorted by exit ID (zeros included) exit_shares (exit_id, n_e / E); null when E = 0 max_exit_share max_e n_e / E; null when E = 0 exit_balance normalized Gini-Simpson index (below); null when K = 1 or E = 0 p_e = n_e / E exit_balance = (1 - Σ_e p_e²) / (1 - 1/K) in [0, 1] exit_balance = 1 when every exit has the same share, and 0 when one exit takes every evacuee. This is descriptive only. Equal use is often not optimal: one exit can be much closer, or threatened by fire. Do not reward or penalize a run for its balance. 10. Replanning and recovery proxies (replanning) These fields count observable reactions to a blocked move. They are proxies. They do not observe model intent, and a model may change its action for reasons that have nothing to do with the block. A blocked event is a decision with a blocked_* outcome. Its next decision is the same person's decision at the next step. It exists only when the person is still active and the episode has not terminated. Field Definition blocked_events number of blocked events (equals movement.blocked_moves) blocks_with_next_decision B' = blocked events that have a next decision blocks_without_next_decision blocked_events - B' moved_after_block next decision has outcome moved (recovery proxy) blocked_after_block next decision is blocked again (repeated-block proxy) stayed_after_block next decision is stay action_changed_after_block next action differs from the blocked action (a change to stay counts) max_consecutive_blocks longest run of consecutive blocked decisions by one person recovery_proxy_rate ratio(moved_after_block, B') repeated_block_proxy_rate ratio(blocked_after_block, B') action_change_proxy_rate ratio(action_changed_after_block, B') Invariant: moved_after_block + blocked_after_block + stayed_after_block = B'. Per person: blocked_moves and max_consecutive_blocks. 11. Rules for any future composite or ranking The metrics deliberately have no single score. Any ranking or composite score built on them MUST meet the rules below. The EMBER Score (scoring.md, scoring version 1.0) states how it meets each rule in its section 13. Any ranking or composite score MUST: be versioned, separately from METRICS_VERSION, and state the exact raw fields and formula it uses; be decomposable: every published composite value must ship with the raw metrics it was computed from; never let speed buy safety: a faster run that is materially less safe (more casualties or stranded people) must never outrank a safer run because of speed alone. Safety outcomes take precedence, for example through a lexicographic order with safety first, not a weighted sum in which time can offset lives. Cross-seed robustness and statistical aggregation are in statistics.md. 12. Per-person fields (people) One PersonMetrics per scenario person, sorted by person ID: Field Definition person_id, initial_position, final_position from the scenario and final_state status terminal status resolution_step evacuation or casualty step; null if stranded exit_id exit used; null unless evacuated casualty_cause cause; null unless a casualty decisions, stay_actions, cells_moved, blocked_moves, max_consecutive_blocks section 6 and 10, for this person time_to_safety τ_i (section 5) static_exit_distance, path_efficiency, detour_ratio section 7 min_fire_distance, fire_exposure section 8 13. Edge cases Case Behaviour Nobody evacuates evacuee statistics, path-efficiency ratios, exit shares and balance are null; person_time_to_safety_total = N · H One exit exit_balance is null No fire ever every person-state is without fire; exposure_total = 0, min_fire_distance = null No movement attempts blocked_rate and congestion_block_rate are null No blocked event with a next decision the three replanning rates are null Person walled off from every exit static_exit_distance = null; the person can never evacuate Episode ends with all_resolved before H non-evacuees are still censored at H, not T Record not terminated, empty, or from another scenario or version MetricsInputError Record consistent but not reproduced by a replay MetricsInputError (record failed simulator replay verification: ...) 14. Serialisation EpisodeMetrics.to_dict() returns plain JSON types. Pairs become objects keyed by ID, outcome, cause or distance (as strings). null marks an undefined ratio. No value is NaN or infinite, so the result encodes with emberbench.canonical.canonical_json.

title: Public scenarios
description: The ten diagnostic scenarios and their design intent.
text: Canonical V1 public scenario suite Field Value Suite ID emberbench-v1-public Suite version 1.0.0 Visibility public (development and diagnostics) Scenario schema 1.0 Location scenarios/public/v1/ Manifest scenarios/public/v1/manifest.json Suite hash 5274d103928e6abbdf8bf761f4cc608eeefc55a802d876a21e878cce9838065b This suite is the fixed, public set of V1 diagnostic scenarios. Each scenario isolates one challenge, so a failure points to one missing capability. The suite uses only the frozen V1 rules in simulation-contract.md and v1-fairness-spec.md. The suite is not the hidden evaluation set. It contains no hidden data, no evaluator seed schedule and no paired seed manifest. A model can be developed against it in the open. Scored evaluation must also use scenarios that are not in this repository. Seeds Every scenario file has a seed, because the schema requires one. In this suite every seed is 0, and the manifest declares "seed_role": "development". The scenario seed is a development default. It makes a local run reproducible. It is not a benchmark seed. Scored seed schedules belong to the evaluator. The evaluator passes them with Simulator(scenario, seed=...). They are never stored here. Paired seed manifests for matched comparison belong to Issue #6. For the nine deterministic scenarios the seed has no effect on the run. For the stochastic scenario (v1-pub-10-route-invalidation) it selects the fire trajectory. A model never receives any seed (see v1-fairness-spec.md, section 1.3). Manifest manifest.json is canonical JSON with a two-space indent and a final newline. emberbench.load_suite(directory) reads it strictly: unknown or missing keys are rejected. It then loads every scenario file with the strict schema parser and checks every pinned field against the file. Key Meaning suite_id, suite_version Suite identity. suite_version is MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. visibility public for this suite. Generated unseen suites use generated (see procedural-generation.md). seed_role Always development. See Seeds. schema_version Scenario schema of every entry. scenarios[] One entry per scenario, sorted by scenario_id. Each entry has: Key Meaning Checked against the file scenario_id Stable ID. Unique. yes path File name, relative to the manifest. Must be <scenario_id>.json. file must exist schema_version Scenario schema version. yes content_hash Scenario.content_hash(): SHA-256 of the canonical scenario JSON. Unique. yes primary_family The main challenge. It is also in families. — families Every family the scenario covers, sorted. — population Number of people. yes exit_count Number of exits. yes ignition_count Number of initial fire cells. yes fire_model deterministic or stochastic. yes purpose One-line diagnostic purpose. — The suite directory must contain only manifest.json and the files that it lists. The suite hash is the SHA-256 of the canonical manifest JSON. It pins every scenario hash and all metadata at once. Design rules Every scenario in the suite follows these rules. tests/test_suite.py checks each of them. It parses under the strict schema V1 parser. It states every configurable rule explicitly: fire.model, fire.spread_interval, fire.exits_flammable, fire.spread_probability (stochastic only), movement.conflict_resolution, movement.enter_fire and termination.max_steps. Every scenario uses enter_fire: "casualty", the V1 default. The file is canonical: it is byte-identical to json.dumps(scenario.to_dict(), indent=2) + "\n", and so a load and save round trip changes nothing. No person starts on a wall, an exit or a fire cell. No two people, exits or ignitions share an ID or a position. Neutral person IDs. IDs are P001 to Pnnn. The number is the rank of sha256("emberbench/v1/public/person-id/{scenario_id}/{row}/{col}"). The ID order is therefore not row-major, and it does not follow the distance to an exit. This matters because the collision rule (R1) uses the ID order. Exit IDs are E1, E2, ... in row-major order of the exit cells. Exit positions are visible to the model anyway. No person is doomed by construction. In every deterministic scenario, each person alone has a fire-free route to some exit in time. Interaction with other people can still cause losses. That is part of the challenge. A scenario adds only the complexity that its challenge needs. This document does not give an optimal action sequence for any scenario, and the tests do not name a winning policy. Family coverage There are twelve required families and ten scenarios. Two scenarios each cover two families. In both cases, the second family is a direct consequence of the first challenge, not an extra one. Family Scenario single_exit_low_density v1-pub-01-single-exit-sparse single_exit_high_density v1-pub-02-single-exit-dense narrow_corridor_bottleneck v1-pub-03-corridor-bottleneck multiple_exits_unequal_distance v1-pub-04-unequal-exits central_ignition v1-pub-05-central-ignition threatened_nearest_exit v1-pub-06-threatened-exit multiple_ignitions v1-pub-07-multiple-ignitions maze_obstacle_routing v1-pub-08-maze-deceptive-exit (primary) deceptive_nearest_exit v1-pub-08-maze-deceptive-exit crowd_100 v1-pub-09-crowd-100-split-flow (primary) split_flow_across_exits v1-pub-09-crowd-100-split-flow route_invalidation_replanning v1-pub-10-route-invalidation Maze and deceptive exit. In V1 an exit can only "deceive" through geometry: the observation shows the full map and the fire. A deceptive exit is therefore one that is near in straight-line distance but far by path. That needs walls that force detours, which is the maze challenge. One scenario tests both: plan with path distance, not straight-line distance. 100-person crowd and split flow. Each exit cell passes one person per step (R4). With 100 people, the queue at one exit is longer than the walk to another exit, so flow allocation is the main difficulty at that scale. A 100-person crowd with one exit would only measure a 100-step queue. Scenarios Hazard notation: det/k is the deterministic model with spread_interval = k. sto/k p is the stochastic model with spread_interval = k and spread_probability = p. "Flammable exits" is fire.exits_flammable. Scenario ID Family Pop. Exits Hazard Intended challenge Why it exists Capability it diagnoses v1-pub-01-single-exit-sparse single exit, low density 4 1 1 ignition, det/3, flammable exits Walk each person to the only exit before a slow fire arrives. Control case. A model that fails here has a basic action or navigation fault. Basic movement, valid actions, shortest-path navigation. v1-pub-02-single-exit-dense single exit, high density 36 1 1 ignition behind the crowd, det/4, flammable exits Drain a packed room through one exit. More people than the longest walk. Separates congestion handling from distance. Queue ordering, collision avoidance, use of the one-person-per-step exit rate. v1-pub-03-corridor-bottleneck narrow corridor bottleneck 8 1 1 ignition at the back of the room, det/2, flammable exits Feed eight people into a one-cell-wide corridor before fire reaches its entrance. Every route shares the same cells, so ordering decides the outcome. Sequencing through restricted geometry under time pressure. v1-pub-04-unequal-exits multiple exits, unequal distance 5 2 1 ignition, det/3, flammable exits Choose between two exits whose path distances differ by at least 4 for each person. Simplest multi-exit decision, with no queue or fire trap. Exit selection by path distance. v1-pub-05-central-ignition central ignition 8 2 1 ignition at the grid centre, det/2, flammable exits Move away from a front that grows in every direction and go around it. The front grows toward people on every side at once. Hazard-aware routing around an expanding front. v1-pub-06-threatened-exit threatened / lost nearest exit 6 2 1 ignition beside the nearest exit, det/2, flammable exits Judge who can still use the nearest exit before it burns, and send the others to the far exit. The nearest exit is a trap for some people and safe for others. Prediction of exit loss from known fire rules; commitment versus switching. v1-pub-07-multiple-ignitions multiple ignitions 9 2 3 separate ignitions, det/3, flammable exits Pass between three growing fronts before they merge. One fire front is not enough to test multi-source threat reasoning. Reasoning about several hazard sources at once. v1-pub-08-maze-deceptive-exit maze / obstacle routing; deceptive nearest exit 5 2 1 ignition in the outer ring, det/3, flammable exits Route through a serpentine maze. The straight-line-nearest exit is far by path. Separates path planning from straight-line heuristics. Path distance around walls; resistance to geometric heuristics. v1-pub-09-crowd-100-split-flow 100-person crowd; split flow 100 3 1 ignition, det/4, flammable exits Evacuate 100 people. Most are nearest to one exit, and its queue is longer than the walk to another exit. Scale test, and the only scenario where flow allocation dominates. Coordination at scale; load balancing across exits. v1-pub-10-route-invalidation route invalidation requiring replanning 6 1 1 ignition in a side shaft, sto/1 p=0.5, non-flammable exits Use or abandon a short corridor that stochastic fire may cut at an unknown time. A longer route stays open. The short route can fail after people commit to it, at a seed-dependent step. Replanning when the current plan becomes invalid; risk under stochastic spread. Each layout below is the static map at step 0: # wall, E exit, F fire (ignition), P person, . floor. Canonical descriptions start with CANONICAL V1 PUBLIC SCENARIO. Change control The suite is frozen at version 1.0.0. tests/test_suite.py pins the suite hash and every scenario hash. Any change to a scenario file changes its content hash. It needs a new suite_version, a new manifest entry and updated pins. Do not edit a scenario in place under the same version. A rule change that changes simulator output bumps SIMULATOR_VERSION. It does not change scenario hashes, because a scenario hash covers only the scenario inputs. title: Running evaluations
description: Paired evaluation schedules, records and result handling.
text: Paired identical evaluation This document specifies how EMBERBench runs several models on exactly the same episodes and how their results are matched. The code is in src/emberbench/evaluation.py. The tests are in tests/test_evaluation.py. Out of scope here: model-provider adapters, win rates, confidence intervals and other aggregate statistics (see statistics.md), procedural scenario generation, held-out integrity and provenance (see integrity.md), and the EMBER Score, leaderboard order and frozen environment packs (see scoring.md and environment-pack.md). 1. Common random numbers An episode is fully defined by a scenario and a seed. All randomness comes from simulator-owned streams derived from the seed (see simulation-contract.md). In V1 the fire does not depend on the actions, so two models that play the same scenario with the same seed face the same fire, cell for cell and step for step. Paired evaluation uses this. Every model plays the same ordered list of (scenario, seed) episodes. A difference between two models on one episode then comes from their decisions only, not from different fire. This is the common-random-numbers method. It removes the between-seed noise from each paired difference, so fewer episodes are necessary to compare two models. The test test_two_policies_see_identical_stochastic_fire checks this on the stochastic scenario v1-pub-10-route-invalidation. A greedy policy and an always-stay policy see identical burning sets at every step that both runs reach, and two different seeds give different fire. 2. The evaluation manifest An EvaluationManifest is an immutable, versioned episode schedule. { "manifest_version": "1.0", "suite_id": "emberbench-v1-public", "suite_version": "1.0.0", "suite_hash": "<sha256 of the canonical suite manifest>", "simulator_version": "0.2.0", "observation_version": "1.0", "metrics_version": "1.0", "episodes": [ {"index": 0, "scenario_id": "v1-pub-01-single-exit-sparse", "scenario_hash": "<sha256>", "seed": 3}, {"index": 1, "scenario_id": "v1-pub-01-single-exit-sparse", "scenario_hash": "<sha256>", "seed": 1} ] } Rules (all enforced on construction and on parsing): manifest_version must be a supported version (1.0). suite_id, suite_version and suite_hash must be well formed. episodes is non-empty. index equals the position in the list (0, 1, 2, ...). Each seed is an integer in [0, 2**64 - 1]. Booleans and floats are rejected. A seed occurs at most once per scenario. The same seed may be used for different scenarios. One scenario ID is pinned to exactly one content hash. Unknown and missing keys are rejected. manifest_hash() is the SHA-256 of the canonical JSON of the whole manifest. A change to any field, any seed, any scenario hash or to the episode order gives a different hash. Building a manifest build_evaluation_manifest(suite, seeds) schedules every suite scenario under every seed: the outer order is the suite manifest order, the inner order is the order of seeds as given. The function does not sort, remove or generate seeds. An empty list, a duplicate or an out-of-range seed is an error. A set, a str or a generator is a TypeError, because it has no reliable order. verify_manifest(manifest, suite) requires that the manifest targets exactly this suite (ID, version, hash) and the running code's simulator, observation and metrics versions, and that every pinned scenario hash matches both the suite entry and the scenario file. run_evaluation and load_evaluation_result always call it. save_evaluation_manifest and load_evaluation_manifest store a manifest as JSON. The loaded manifest is checked with the same rules. 3. Public development manifests and private scored manifests The seeds decide the fire. If a model developer knows the scored seeds, they can tune a model to that exact fire. Therefore: Development manifests use small, fixed, public seeds (for example [0, 1, 2]). They are fine in tests, examples and documentation. The test suite pins one: the public suite under seeds (0, 1, 2) has manifest hash 7b9aae45e5e2828f881b2f14d8e5585627e5f8bdbb137a1ed2331bf10ce8c876. Scored manifests use high-entropy seeds chosen by the evaluator (for example 64-bit values from secrets.randbits(64)). The evaluator keeps the seed schedule outside this repository and publishes the manifest, if at all, only after the evaluation. This repository never generates scored seeds. The seed in a scenario file is a development default only. run_evaluation always overrides it with the manifest seed. A published manifest hash lets anyone check later that a published schedule is the one that was used, without revealing the seeds before the evaluation. 4. Seed privacy and episode isolation The evaluator knows the manifest and the seeds. The decision policy does not. run_evaluation(suite, manifest, model_id, policy_factory, output_path, resume=True) does this for each episode: policy = policy_factory(). The factory receives no arguments: no scenario, seed, episode index or other metadata. run_episode(scenario, policy, seed=episode.seed). The policy is called with exactly one positional argument, an Observation, once per step. The policy never receives the EvaluationManifest, an episode entry or index, the seed, the Scenario, the Simulator, the RunRecord or any evaluator metadata. The Observation contains no seed and no RNG state (see v1-fairness-spec.md). A new policy is built for every episode, so state that a policy keeps cannot carry over into the next episode. This also makes resume correct: an episode gives the same result whether it runs in a fresh process or after other episodes. The factory must return a new policy each time. A plain stateless function is also acceptable. The tests prove this: test_policy_receives_only_observations uses a policy that records every argument it receives and a factory that records its own arguments. The factory is called with () once per episode. Each policy call has exactly one argument of type Observation and no keyword arguments. Every object inside the observation is one of the known observation types. The 64-bit seed (in decimal and hex), the manifest hash, the suite hash and the scenario hashes do not occur in its JSON form. test_fresh_policy_per_episode checks that there is one distinct policy instance per episode and that each instance sees one episode, from step 0. Limit: this is an interface contract for in-process Python policies, not a sandbox. Python code can inspect its caller's stack. A real model adapter must send only the serialized observation to the model. For per-episode agents, action validation, optional execution accounting and the canonical serialized observation, see model-interface.md. 5. The per-model result artifact run_evaluation writes one JSON artifact per model run. It is canonical JSON (sorted keys, no extra whitespace) followed by a newline. { "result_version": "1.0", "model_id": "model-a", "evaluation_manifest_hash": "<sha256>", "suite_id": "emberbench-v1-public", "suite_version": "1.0.0", "suite_hash": "<sha256>", "simulator_version": "0.2.0", "observation_version": "1.0", "metrics_version": "1.0", "manifest": { "...": "the complete evaluation manifest" }, "episodes": [ { "index": 0, "scenario_id": "v1-pub-01-single-exit-sparse", "scenario_hash": "<sha256>", "seed": 3, "record_digest": "<sha256 of the canonical run record>", "record": { "...": "the complete RunRecord" }, "metrics": { "...": "EpisodeMetrics.to_dict()" } } ] } The header fields repeat the embedded manifest so a reader can see them at once. They must equal the manifest. episodes holds completed episodes only, in manifest order. Each one names its exact manifest entry and contains the full RunRecord, so anyone can replay and audit it, plus the raw metrics computed from it. model_id is a label chosen by the evaluator (1 to 256 printable characters, no leading or trailing whitespace). It is not proof of which model produced the actions, and it is not a unique key. load_evaluation_result(path, suite) accepts an artifact only if all of these hold: the JSON has exactly the expected keys at every level; the embedded manifest is valid, its hash equals evaluation_manifest_hash, and every header field equals the manifest; the manifest passes verify_manifest against suite and the running code; every episode index is in the manifest, occurs once, and episodes are in manifest order; every episode's scenario_id, scenario_hash and seed equal its manifest entry, and the record's header agrees with them; every record is in canonical form and matches record_digest; every record is authenticated: compute_episode_metrics checks its structure and replays its action log in a fresh simulator, which must reproduce it byte for byte; every stored metrics object equals the metrics recomputed from the authenticated record; the artifact as a whole re-serializes to exactly the loaded JSON. Any failure raises EvaluationError. Nothing is repaired, skipped or ignored. 6. Resume guarantees run_evaluation saves the artifact after every completed episode. Each save writes a temporary file in the same directory, flushes and fsyncs it, and renames it over the artifact with os.replace. A crash therefore leaves either the previous artifact or the new one, never a partial file. After a hard crash (for example a power loss) a stray .<name>.*.tmp file can remain next to the artifact. It is never read and can be deleted. If the output path does not exist, an artifact with zero episodes is written before the first episode runs. If output_path exists: With resume=False it is an error. An existing artifact is never overwritten. With resume=True (the default) the artifact is loaded and authenticated completely, as in section 5. Then it must have the same evaluation manifest hash and the same model ID as the call. A changed schedule, seed order, scenario, suite or version, or a different model ID, is rejected. Only the episodes that are not in the artifact run, in manifest order. A completed episode is never run again. Because each episode uses a fresh policy and its own seed, an interrupted and resumed run gives the same artifact, byte for byte, as an uninterrupted run with a deterministic policy. test_interrupted_run_resumes_without_rerunning checks this. A policy exception or an invalid action stops the run with that exception. The artifact keeps the episodes completed before it. Cost note: the whole artifact is rewritten after each episode, so total bytes written grow with the square of the number of episodes. This is acceptable for V1 schedules. A sharded layout can replace it later without changing the pairing rules. 7. Exact pairing pair_results(a, b) compares two loaded artifacts. It first requires that both use the same evaluation manifest (equal hash and equal content). Otherwise it raises EvaluationError: results from different schedules are never compared. Each scheduled episode has the key (evaluation manifest hash, episode index, scenario ID, scenario hash, seed) Definition. An episode is a comparable pair exactly when both artifacts contain a result whose key equals that scheduled key. Nothing else (model ID, file name, run order or time) is part of the key. The function returns a PairingReport: Field Meaning manifest_hash the shared evaluation manifest hash model_a, model_b the two model ID labels total_scheduled number of episodes in the manifest paired keys present in both artifacts, in manifest order paired_count len(paired) missing_from_a scheduled keys that a does not have missing_from_b scheduled keys that b does not have An episode that neither artifact has is in both missing lists. The report holds no scores, win rates or statistics. statistics.md defines the paired statistics; they use only paired episodes. 8. Example from emberbench import build_evaluation_manifest, load_suite, pair_results, run_evaluation suite = load_suite("scenarios/public/v1") manifest = build_evaluation_manifest(suite, [0, 1, 2]) # development seeds def make_policy(): # Return a NEW policy. It receives only Observation values. return MyPolicy() a = run_evaluation(suite, manifest, "model-a", make_policy, "results/model-a.json") b = run_evaluation(suite, manifest, "model-b", make_other_policy, "results/model-b.json") report = pair_results(a, b) print(report.total_scheduled, report.paired_count) To compare saved artifacts later, load each with load_evaluation_result(path, suite), which authenticates every record, and then call pair_results.

title: Frozen environments
description: EnvironmentPack construction, digests and matched fire worlds.
text: Frozen environment packs (environment pack version 1.0) An environment pack freezes the complete evaluation environment once, before any model runs. Every model is then evaluated on the same bytes, the same seed schedule and the same fire worlds. The code is src/emberbench/environment_pack.py. The tests are tests/test_environment_pack.py. The score that uses a pack is in scoring.md. 1. What a pack freezes Part Content Scenario bytes an exact byte copy of every scenario file and of the suite manifest.json Generator record for a generated suite, the exact generation.json (generator version, config, batch, pinned proxies) Seed schedule the ordered evaluation-manifest.json (episode index, scenario ID, scenario hash, seed) Fire worlds one fire_world_digest per scheduled episode Versions pack_versions(): environment pack, simulator, observation, action schema, scenario schema, metrics, generator, generator config, generation manifest and evaluation manifest File hashes the SHA-256 of every file in the pack Pack digest SHA-256 of the canonical JSON of pack.json pack.json lists the SHA-256 of every other file, so the pack digest pins every byte of the pack. 2. Layout <pack>/ pack.json the record; its canonical digest is the pack digest evaluation-manifest.json the ordered seed schedule suite/ a plain suite: manifest.json + scenario files generated-suite/ or a generated suite: generation.json suite/ pack.json has exactly these keys: environment_pack_version, pack_id, source (suite or generated_suite), versions, suite (ID, version, suite hash, and per scenario its ID, content hash and primary family), evaluation_manifest_hash, episodes (per episode: index, scenario ID, scenario hash, seed, fire_world_digest) and files (sorted [path, sha256] pairs). 3. API from emberbench import freeze_environment_pack, load_environment_pack, verify_environment_pack pack = freeze_environment_pack(suite_or_frozen_generated_suite, [seed0, seed1, ...], "packs/2026-q4", pack_id="2026-q4") digest = pack.digest # publish this before the evaluation pack = load_environment_pack("packs/2026-q4", expected_digest=digest) verify_environment_pack("packs/2026-q4", expected_digest=digest) # returns the digest or raises freeze_environment_pack(source, schedule, directory, *, pack_id). source is a loaded Suite or a FrozenGeneratedSuite. schedule is an ordered seed list (scheduled with build_evaluation_manifest) or an existing EvaluationManifest that targets the suite. The directory must not exist or must be empty: a pack is never overwritten. The pack is written to a temporary sibling, renamed into place, then loaded back and verified from disk. load_environment_pack(directory, *, expected_digest=None) verifies and returns an EnvironmentPack (suite, manifest, generation, episodes, record, digest). verify_environment_pack(directory, *, expected_digest=None) returns the digest or raises. fire_world_digest(scenario, seed) is the SHA-256 of the canonical JSON of the scenario hash, the seed and the sorted burning cells of every snapshot 0..H. Because it includes the seed, two seeds always give two digests, also when their fire trajectories are equal. environment_world_digest(scenario, seed) (module emberbench.worlds) is the seed-free world identity: the SHA-256 of the canonical JSON of the environment-world version, the simulator and observation versions, the scenario hash and the sorted burning cells of every snapshot 0..H. Two episodes have the same digest exactly when they give a policy the same environment. A deterministic-fire scenario is one world for every seed. build_unique_world_manifest(suite, candidate_seeds, *, stochastic_worlds) schedules each deterministic-fire scenario once (first candidate seed) and each stochastic-fire scenario with the first stochastic_worlds candidate seeds that give pairwise-different environment worlds. It raises EvaluationError when the candidates have too few different worlds. The result is a normal EvaluationManifest, so it freezes into a pack like any other schedule. build_evaluation_manifest is unchanged and still schedules the full scenario x seed product. The pack ID is 1 to 128 ASCII letters, digits, -, _ or .. 4. Verification fails closed load_environment_pack raises EnvironmentPackError when any of these is true: pack.json is missing, is not JSON, or has a missing or extra key; the pack version or any entry of versions differs from the running code; a listed file is missing, a file is not listed, a path is unsafe, or a symbolic link is present; a file's SHA-256 differs from its listed value; the suite does not load (load_suite) or the generated suite does not verify (load_generated_suite); the evaluation manifest does not target the suite (verify_manifest) or its hash differs; the record differs from the record rebuilt from the files, including any fire world recomputed from the scenario and the seed; expected_digest is given and differs. score_results(..., pack) also refuses results whose manifest is not the pack's manifest, and checks every episode's fire trajectory against the pack. 5. Identical environments for every model Never regenerated per model. A pack is written once. Models only read it. A model's score names the pack digest; two scores are comparable only with the same digest. No model-dependent state. In V1 the fire ignores people and actions. The burning set of every snapshot is a function of the scenario and the seed (oracle.fire_trajectory). The pack stores its digest, and scoring checks every recorded snapshot against it. So every model meets the same fire at the same step: common random numbers by construction. Nothing in the pack depends on a model or on any mid-episode state that a model can change. People are the model's. Positions, blocks and outcomes depend on the model's actions. They are in the run record and are authenticated by replay; they are not in the pack. 6. API and external models An external model (an LLM API or any remote service) is a policy behind the adapter of model-interface.md: The evaluator holds the pack. The model never receives the pack, the seed, the fire trajectory or any privileged reference. At each step the model receives one Observation and returns one ActionOutput. Invalid output raises ModelOutputError; the episode is declared invalid_output and scores 0. The evaluator runs the simulator locally and records the run. Scoring is local, from replayed records only. Provider-reported success, accuracy, safety or cost is never trusted and never used. Cost for the EMBER-Efficiency view is measured by the evaluator. A timeout is the adapter's own deadline. A timed-out episode is declared timeout and scores 0. Provider retries are an adapter policy, recorded in the run's configuration, not hidden. A model error (the provider or the adapter raised) is declared model_error and scores 0. A failure can never disappear: an episode without a result and without a declaration is missing and scores 0. Operational data is recorded separately in an OperationalRecord (scoring.md, section 11): model ID, provider ID, the inference configuration digest, latency, input tokens, output tokens, cost and its unit, retries and timeouts. It is never a score input. Stochasticity protocol. Pin the inference configuration (model name and version or snapshot, temperature, top-p, max tokens, system prompt, adapter version) and record it with the submission as inference_config_digest(config). All trials of one submission use the same digest. temperature = 0 is not a determinism guarantee. Batching, numerics and provider-side changes can change outputs. Run K >= 3 trials of the full pack for any sampled model (K = 1 only for a policy shown to be deterministic). Score them together with score_results([trial_1, ..., trial_K], pack). Each episode is the mean of its trials. Report K. Never select the best trial. Every trial that started is scored; a trial that failed contributes zeros. 7. Privacy and publication A pack contains the evaluator seeds and, for a held-out generated suite, the private scenarios. It is a private asset until the evaluation ends (see integrity.md). Publish the pack digest first, as a commitment. Publish the pack after the evaluation; anyone can then run verify_environment_pack with the published digest and re-score every submitted result. 8. Versioning ENVIRONMENT_PACK_VERSION = "1.0". It changes when the layout, the record or the fire-world digest changes. The scoring correction pass (person-level attribution, severe quality gates, the exit-capacity time bound) changed none of these, so the version stays "1.0": the privileged references are recomputed by the scorer from the pack, and are not stored in it. A pack is valid only under the exact versions in its versions entry; a simulator or schema change invalidates every pack, by design.

title: Simulation contract
description: Movement, collisions, exits and fire semantics.
text: Simulation contract (simulator version 0.2.0) This document is normative. If the code and this document disagree, it is a bug. The V1 fairness contract, the model-visible observation and the rationale for each frozen rule are in v1-fairness-spec.md. A change to any rule that changes output for the same inputs must bump SIMULATOR_VERSION in src/emberbench/__init__.py. Coordinates and neighbourhood A position is [row, col], and [0, 0] is the top-left cell. north is row − 1, south is row + 1, west is col − 1, east is col + 1. The neighbourhood is von Neumann (4-connected). Diagonal moves and diagonal fire spread do not exist. Canonical order is row-major (sort by row, then by column). Person and exit IDs sort as plain strings by code point, so "P10" < "P2". State A SimState snapshot contains: step, every person (id, position, status), the burning cells, the trapped set, the RNG stream positions, terminated and termination_reason. Snapshots are frozen dataclasses. Two equal snapshots serialise to identical canonical JSON. A SimState is evaluator-private. A decision model sees only the Observation (see v1-fairness-spec.md). The person status is one of active, evacuated or casualty. A resolved person stays in the record with its last position, but it does not occupy a cell any more and must not receive actions. At the start of every step, no active person stands on an exit or on a burning cell. Phase order Each Simulator.step(actions) runs these phases in this order: # Phase Rule 1 Observation observe() returns the pre-step model-visible Observation: step, static map, episode rules, people, burning cells and allowed actions. It never includes the seed, RNG state, hidden scenario metadata or the trapped set. 2 Actions The mapping must have exactly one entry per active person. Values are stay/north/south/east/west (or Action). Anything else raises InvalidActionError, and the state does not change. 3 Movement validation stay gives stayed. A move off the grid gives blocked_boundary. A move into an obstacle gives blocked_wall. A move into a burning cell gives blocked_fire if movement.enter_fire = "blocked". Otherwise the move continues. 4 Collision resolution See Collisions. 5 Movement All moves resolved as moved happen at once. 6 Evacuation Every active person on an exit that was not burning at the start of the step is evacuated and recorded with the exit ID. 7 Fire propagation The fire model returns newly ignited cells for step number t (1-based). 8 Casualties and trapping Every still-active person on a burning cell becomes a casualty. The cause is entered_fire if the cell was burning before phase 7, else fire_spread. Then the trapped set is recomputed. 9 Termination If no person is active, the reason is all_resolved. Else, if t >= termination.max_steps, the reason is max_steps. all_resolved wins when both hold. A terminated simulator raises SimulationError on step(). Consequences of the order: Evacuation (6) comes before fire spread (7). A person who reaches an exit in the same step that the fire reaches it gets out. Casualties (8) come after fire spread (7). A person who does not move away from a cell that ignites this step dies. Collisions Collision resolution uses these rules in this order. Each rule only looks at movers that are still unresolved. Occupied by a non-mover. If the target holds a person who is not trying to move (stay, or blocked in phase 3), the move gives blocked_occupied. Same target. If two or more movers target one cell, the lowest ID wins. Every other mover gives blocked_conflict. This is decided on intent only. A loser is not re-awarded the cell if the winner fails later. Chains. A winner moves if its target is empty, or if the target's occupant moves out successfully in the same step. People can follow each other in one step (a b . E: both move east). If the chain ends at a person who does not move, every mover in the chain gives blocked_occupied. Cycles. Swaps (A <-> B) and longer rotations are never allowed. Every member gives blocked_cycle. A blocked person stays in its cell. The outcome does not depend on the order in which actions are submitted. Exits are normal cells for movement. Each exit cell therefore lets at most one person through per step: two people who target the same exit are a normal conflict. Because people leave in phase 6, an exit is always empty at the start of the next step. Entering fire. movement.enter_fire is either blocked or casualty. With blocked, the move into fire is refused (blocked_fire). With casualty, the person moves and dies in phase 8 (entered_fire). This includes a burning exit: a burning exit never evacuates anyone. Fire The fire model interface is in src/emberbench/fire.py: class FireModel(Protocol): name: str # read-only def spread(self, terrain: FireTerrain, burning: frozenset[Pos], step: int, rng: SplitMix64) -> frozenset[Pos]: ... Contract: The model returns only cells that are not burning and that are flammable. The simulator checks this and raises SimulationError on a violation. Walls never burn, and fire never passes through them. Spread is only into flammable 4-neighbours of burning cells. Exits burn only if fire.exits_flammable = true. A burning exit stays burning and cannot evacuate anyone. With false, exits never ignite. Validation then rejects an ignition point on an exit. Cells burn forever (no burn-out in V1). People do not block fire. Spread happens only on steps where step % fire.spread_interval == 0. Randomness comes only from the passed rng, which is the simulator's fire stream. The model draws in canonical order. V1 models: deterministic: on a spread step, every flammable neighbour of a burning cell ignites. stochastic: on a spread step, each (candidate cell, burning neighbour) edge takes one Bernoulli(spread_probability) draw. The order is candidates row-major, then sources row-major. A candidate ignites if any of its edges succeeds. All draws are always taken, so the stream position depends only on the geometry. With p = 1 the result equals deterministic. With p = 0 there is no spread. Stochastic fire (frozen V1 contract) Frontier. Before a spread step t, let B be the burning set. A candidate is a cell c that is not in B, is not a wall, is not a non-flammable exit, and has at least one 4-neighbour in B. An edge is a pair (c, s) with c a candidate and s a burning 4-neighbour of c. A candidate has k edges, with 1 <= k <= 4. Draw order. Edges are visited in canonical order: candidates in row-major order, then, for each candidate, its sources in row-major order. Each edge takes exactly one bernoulli(p) from the simulator's fire stream, with p = fire.spread_probability. c ignites in step t if at least one of its edges succeeds. Every edge of every candidate is drawn, also after an earlier edge of the same candidate succeeded. Probability. The draws for the k edges of c are consecutive outputs of the specified PRNG stream, so under the model of independent Bernoulli(p) draws: P(c ignites at step t | B) = 1 - (1 - p)^k p = 0 gives no spread. p = 1 gives exactly the deterministic result on spread steps. "Independent" means sequential draws from the specified SplitMix64 stream. It is a modelling statement about the generator, not a claim of physical independence between neighbouring flames. Exactly: bernoulli(p) is u / 2**53 < p, where u = next_u64() >> 11 takes the values 0 .. 2**53 - 1. So exactly ceil(p * 2**53) of the 2**53 values succeed. For p = 0 this is none, and for p = 1 it is all. Draw-consumption rule. Let E_t be the number of edges of the frontier of B before step t. The fire stream advances by exactly draws(t) = E_t if t % spread_interval == 0 draws(t) = 0 otherwise for every p in [0, 1], including p = 0 and p = 1. No candidates means zero draws. The deterministic model never draws. Actions, people, action mapping order and the construction order of B cannot change the stream position. SplitMix64 adds a fixed constant to its state per draw, so the draw count between two recorded rng_state values can be computed exactly; the tests do this for every step of recorded runs. Golden traces. tests/fixtures/golden/stochastic_fire_traces.json pins five short fire traces (8 to 12 steps). Each pins the scenario hash, seed, ignited cells per step, draws per step, final burning set and final fire RNG state. The same values must come out on every platform and Python version. Not in V1 V1 fire semantics, the scenario schema and the model-visible RulesView are frozen. V1 does not support, and FireConfig and RulesView have no fields for: delayed ignition events after step 0 (all ignitions burn at step 0); wind or other directional spread probabilities; burn-out (cells burn until the end of the run, R8); smoke or visibility effects; material-specific flammability (every non-wall cell is flammable, except exits when exits_flammable is false); fire that depends on people or actions. These are future-version features. Each one changes simulator output or the model-visible rules, so it needs a new SIMULATOR_VERSION and, where the rules change, a new OBSERVATION_VERSION and scenario schema version. Issue #7 mentions optional directional parameters and delayed-ignition behaviour; the decision is to defer both to a future version to keep the frozen V1 contract. Randomness The only generator is emberbench.rng.SplitMix64. It is fully specified in code, and a test checks it against the reference output. Stream seeds are sha256("emberbench/v1/{seed}/{label}")[:8] (big-endian). V1 has one stream, fire. A new subsystem gets a new label, so it does not shift the existing streams. bernoulli(p) always consumes exactly one draw and compares a 53-bit dyadic float with p. It uses no other floating-point arithmetic. The stream positions are part of SimState (for audit and resume). They are not part of Observation. The fire stream is exogenous: the fire model never sees people or actions. For the same scenario and seed, every action sequence gives the same fire trajectory on the steps that the runs share. Trapping trapped is the set of active people with no path to a non-burning exit. A path may cross any cell that is not a wall and not burning. Other people are ignored. This is an evaluator diagnostic for later metrics. It is not in the Observation. It does not change the person's status or end the run. Replay RunRecord stores the header (simulator_version, observation_version, schema_version, scenario_id, scenario_hash, seed), the initial state, and for each step the actions, resolved movements, ignitions, evacuations, casualties and the post-step state. verify_record(scenario, record) checks the simulator version, the observation version and the scenario hash. It then replays the recorded actions and requires a byte-identical canonical encoding. It reports the first step that diverges.

title: Fairness specification
description: Information boundaries and the frozen V1 protocol.
text: EMBERBench V1 fairness and semantics specification This document is normative. It freezes the V1 fairness contract, the model-visible observation and the V1 simulator rules. The words MUST, MUST NOT and SHOULD have their RFC 2119 meaning. Contract Version Defined in Simulator semantics and run record format SIMULATOR_VERSION = "0.2.0" src/emberbench/__init__.py, simulation-contract.md Scenario schema SCHEMA_VERSION = "1.0" src/emberbench/scenario.py, scenario-schema.md Model-visible observation OBSERVATION_VERSION = "1.0" src/emberbench/observation.py, this document If the code and this document disagree, it is a bug. V1 in one sentence. A model sees the full current state and knows the episode dynamics (the rules). The evaluator's randomness (the seed, the RNG state and every future draw) stays hidden. V1 evaluates decisions under known rules, not inference of hidden rules. 1. Fairness contract 1.1 Matched evaluation Every compared model MUST run on exactly the same: scenario (the same Scenario.content_hash()), simulator version (SIMULATOR_VERSION), initial population, with the same person IDs and positions, hazard configuration (ignitions, fire model and its parameters), evaluator seed schedule (the same list of seeds for each scenario), exogenous stochastic process (the fire RNG stream derived from each seed). The only input that differs between two matched runs is the sequence of actions that the models submit. A RunRecord header (simulator_version, observation_version, scenario_hash, seed) identifies the matched episode and the observation contract the model received. 1.2 Evaluator-private and model-visible state The simulator state has two separate parts. Evaluator-private state. Only the evaluator and the harness may read it. A decision model MUST NOT receive any of it, in any form, before or during a run: Item Where it lives Evaluator seed, and Scenario.seed Simulator.seed, Scenario, RunRecord.seed RNG stream positions and stream seeds SimState.rng_state Future random draws the fire stream (SplitMix64) Scenario ID, description, content hash, schema version Scenario, RunRecord header trapped diagnostic SimState.trapped The full state, the step log and the run record SimState, StepRecord, RunRecord The Scenario and Simulator objects evaluator side Model-visible state. A decision model receives only the Observation returned by Simulator.observe(). Section 4 defines its fields. It has the full current state (map, people, fire) and the episode rules (RulesView): every action-relevant rule that a scenario can vary. The rules are copied from the scenario, so the model never holds a Scenario reference. The harness boundary is Simulator.observe() and Simulator.step(actions). A harness MUST give a model only Observation objects (or their to_dict() form). It MUST NOT give a model the Simulator, the Scenario, a SimState, a StepRecord or a RunRecord until the evaluation is complete. run_episode(scenario, policy) obeys this rule: the policy receives only Observation objects. 1.3 The seed The seed exists for reproducibility and for matched evaluation only. It is not a model input. The evaluator owns the seed schedule. The schedule MUST NOT be disclosed to a model before the evaluation is complete. Scored evaluations SHOULD draw seeds uniformly from [0, 2**64) with a cryptographic generator. A model that knows the simulator code could test small seeds (0, 1, 2, ...) against the fire it observes and then predict future fire. A 64-bit seed space, with stream seeds derived by SHA-256, makes that search impractical. The small seeds in tests/fixtures/ are for tests only. A model sees the realised fire (the burning cells). That is the intended information. It does not see the draws that produced the fire, or any future draw. 1.4 Person and exit IDs Person IDs and exit IDs are model-visible, because actions are keyed by person ID. Scenario authors MUST NOT encode hidden test-set metadata in them. IDs SHOULD carry no information about the solution (for example, IDs SHOULD NOT be ordered by distance to an exit), because the collision rule (R1) uses the ID order. 2. Stochastic-world fairness Fire is exogenous in V1. People and actions do not affect fire propagation: The fire model receives only the static terrain, the burning cells, the step number and the fire RNG stream (FireModel.spread). It does not receive people or actions. People do not block fire, and fire spread does not depend on where people are. The stochastic model takes one draw per (candidate cell, burning neighbour) edge on every spread step. The number of draws depends only on the geometry and the burning set. Therefore, for the same scenario and the same evaluator seed, two runs with different actions MUST produce identical ignitions, burning sets and fire RNG positions on every step that both runs complete. The fire trajectory is equal to the trajectory the fire process produces with no people at all. This is the "common random numbers" property: a difference in outcome between two matched runs comes from the decisions only, not from luck. A run can end earlier than another run (for example when everyone evacuates). The invariant holds for the overlapping steps. The exact probability and draw-count rules are in simulation-contract.md. Tests: test_stochastic_hazard.py checks the invariant for stay, greedy, deliberately conflicting, all-east and random policies against the fire with no people at all. It uses several development seeds on multiple ignitions, flammable and non-flammable exits, spread_interval 2, p = 0, p = 1 and the public route-invalidation scenario. It compares ignitions, burning sets and the fire RNG state on every step. See also test_fairness.py::test_fire_trajectory_*. A future subsystem that needs randomness MUST use a new stream label (see simulation-contract.md). If its draws depend on actions, it MUST NOT share a stream with the fire. 3. Frozen V1 rules Each rule has a short rationale and the tests that pin it. V1 keeps the Phase 1 behaviour for every rule. No rule changed in Phase 2: the simulator dynamics are the same as in 0.1.0. SIMULATOR_VERSION is 0.2.0 only because the RunRecord header gained observation_version (see section 6). Every rule that a scenario can vary is in Observation.rules. The model knows the rules it plays under. R1. Collision tie-break: lowest person ID wins If two or more movers target the same cell, the mover with the lowest person ID wins. IDs compare as plain strings by code point ("P10" < "P2"). Every other mover gets blocked_conflict. The decision uses intent only. A loser is not re-awarded the cell if the winner fails later. Rationale. The rule is deterministic, simple and visible to the model (IDs are in the observation, and rules.conflict_resolution names the rule). It is identical for every model on a scenario. A random tie-break would need RNG draws whose count depends on the actions. That would either couple the fire stream to the actions (section 2) or add a second stream with no benefit for fairness. The known bias (low IDs win) is the same for every compared model. Tests: test_v1_rules.py::test_r1_*, test_movement.py::test_conflict_lowest_id_wins_regardless_of_submission_order, test_movement.py::test_ids_compare_as_strings, test_movement.py::test_conflict_loser_is_not_reawarded_when_winner_fails. R2. Swaps are blocked Two people who try to exchange cells (A <-> B) both get blocked_cycle and stay in place. Rationale. A cell holds one person. A swap needs two people to pass through each other on a shared edge. This is not possible in a one-cell-wide corridor, and the grid cannot tell a wide passage from a narrow one. Blocking is the conservative, simple rule. Tests: test_v1_rules.py::test_r2_*, test_movement.py::test_swap_is_blocked. R3. Rotations are blocked Any closed chain of movers (a rotation of length 3 or more) is blocked. Every member gets blocked_cycle. An outside mover with a lower ID than the cycle member it meets wins the conflict (R1). That cycle member then becomes a non-mover, and the chain resolves as blocked_occupied. Rationale. Same rule as R2, with no special case. Open chains (people who follow each other in one step) are allowed, so a queue still moves at full speed. Tests: test_v1_rules.py::test_r3_*, test_movement.py::test_rotation_is_blocked, test_movement.py::test_lower_id_outsider_breaks_rotation, test_movement.py::test_following_chain_moves_together. R4. Exit throughput: one person per exit cell per step An exit is a normal cell for movement, with capacity one. A person who moves onto a usable exit is evacuated in the same step (phase 6). The exit is therefore empty at the start of the next step. Each exit cell lets at most one person through per step. A queue flows with no gaps: the next person can move into the vacated cell in the same step. Two adjacent exit cells let two people through per step. Rationale. Throughput follows from the one-person-per-cell rule. It needs no extra parameter. Congestion at exits is part of what V1 measures. Tests: test_v1_rules.py::test_r4_*, test_simulator.py::test_exit_throughput_is_one_person_per_exit_per_step, test_simulator.py::test_two_people_cannot_enter_one_exit_in_the_same_step. R5. Burning exits are unusable An exit evacuates a person only if the exit was not burning at the start of the step. A burning exit never evacuates anyone. Moving onto a burning exit follows R6: it is refused (blocked) or the person becomes a casualty (casualty). An exit can burn only if fire.exits_flammable is true. A person who reaches an exit in the same step that the fire reaches it is evacuated, because evacuation (phase 6) comes before fire spread (phase 7). Rationale. A burning exit is the main "exit becomes unusable" event that V1 measures. Evacuation before spread gives the model the benefit of the doubt for a move that was valid when it was chosen: the model saw a usable exit. Tests: test_v1_rules.py::test_r5_*, test_simulator.py::test_entering_burning_exit_does_not_evacuate, test_fire.py::test_exit_flammability_is_configurable, test_fire.py::test_fire_threatening_exit_burns_exit_and_it_stops_evacuating. R6. enter_fire: explicit in every scenario, default casualty movement.enter_fire is blocked or casualty. With blocked, a move into a cell that was burning at the start of the step gives blocked_fire, and the person stays in place. With casualty, the person moves and becomes a casualty with cause entered_fire. Scenario files MUST state the value (the key is required). The Python default (MovementConfig()) is casualty. Scored V1 scenarios SHOULD use casualty. Rationale. casualty makes a bad decision have its real consequence, so it measures decision quality. blocked hides some bad decisions behind a safety net. Both values stay available for tests and ablations, and the value is part of the scenario hash, so two runs can never silently use different policies. Tests: test_v1_rules.py::test_r6_*, test_movement.py::test_enter_fire_policies, test_simulator.py::test_entering_fire_under_casualty_policy, test_simulator.py::test_blocked_fire_policy_keeps_person_in_place. R7. Ignition timing The scenario ignitions burn at step 0. They are in the first observation. No person can start on an ignition. Spread happens in phase 7 of step t (1-based), only when t % fire.spread_interval == 0. The first possible spread is in step spread_interval. Movement (phase 5) happens before spread (phase 7) in the same step. A person who moves away from a cell that ignites in this step survives. A person who stays on it becomes a casualty with cause fire_spread. Cells that ignite in step t are in the observation before step t + 1. Rationale. The model always acts on the fire it can see. No cell burns "between" the observation and the move. Tests: test_v1_rules.py::test_r7_*, test_fire.py::test_spread_interval, test_simulator.py::test_fire_spread_casualty_and_cause. R8. No burn-out A burning cell burns until the end of the run. Burn-out does not exist in V1, for any cell type (floor or exit). The burning set never shrinks. Rationale. Simple and monotone. A burned-out cell that becomes passable again would add a timing rule and new routing behaviour that V1 does not need. A later version can add burn-out with a SIMULATOR_VERSION bump. Tests: test_v1_rules.py::test_r8_*. R9. Trapped definition trapped is the set of active people who have no path to an exit that is not burning. A path uses 4-neighbour steps and may cross any cell that is not a wall and not burning. Other people are ignored. The set is computed at step 0 and after phase 8 of every step. trapped is an evaluator diagnostic. It is recorded in SimState and RunRecord. It is not model-visible in V1. It does not change a person's status, and it does not end the run. Rationale. Walls and fire are permanent in V1 (R8). People are not, so congestion does not count as trapped. The diagnostic is for metrics (for example "trapped from the start" against "trapped by a bad decision"). It is kept out of the observation because it is a pre-computed planning aid. A model can compute the same set from the observation (the map plus the burning cells), so hiding it removes no information. Tests: test_v1_rules.py::test_r9_*, test_simulator.py::test_trapped_detection, test_fairness.py::test_trapped_diagnostic_is_evaluator_private. R10. Termination precedence After phase 8 of step t: If no person is active, the run ends with all_resolved. Else, if t >= termination.max_steps, the run ends with max_steps. all_resolved wins when both hold. Inside a step, evacuation (phase 6) comes before casualties (phase 8). A run does not end early because every active person is trapped. A terminated simulator raises SimulationError on step(). Rationale. A run that resolves everyone on its last step is a full success, so all_resolved is the more informative reason. Early stop on "all trapped" would make the run length depend on a diagnostic. It would not change any outcome, because a trapped person cannot evacuate. Tests: test_v1_rules.py::test_r10_*, test_simulator.py::test_all_resolved_takes_precedence_over_max_steps, test_simulator.py::test_max_steps_termination_is_deterministic. 4. Observation contract (version 1.0) Simulator.observe() returns an Observation. In V1 the current state is fully observable (the observation shows every burning cell) and the episode dynamics are known (rules). The observation holds no reference to the scenario, the simulator or any RNG. Its object graph contains only these types: Observation, MapView, RulesView, ExitSpec, PersonState, PersonStatus, Action, Pos, FireModelName, EnterFirePolicy, ConflictResolution, tuples, frozensets, integers, floats, booleans, strings and None. Field Type Meaning step int Number of completed steps. 0 before the first step. map.width, map.height int Grid size. map.obstacles tuple[Pos, ...] Wall cells, row-major. map.exits tuple[ExitSpec, ...] Exit ID and position, sorted by ID. rules RulesView The episode dynamics. See the next table. people tuple[PersonState, ...] Every person: id, position, status (active, evacuated, casualty), sorted by ID. burning frozenset[Pos] Every burning cell now. allowed_actions tuple[Action, ...] stay, north, south, east, west. Every active person may submit any of them every step. RulesView holds every action-relevant rule that a scenario can vary. Each value is copied from the scenario when the simulator is built: Field Type Copied from fire_model FireModelName fire.model (deterministic or stochastic) spread_interval int fire.spread_interval spread_probability float | None fire.spread_probability. None (JSON null) unless the model is stochastic. exits_flammable bool fire.exits_flammable enter_fire EnterFirePolicy movement.enter_fire (blocked or casualty) conflict_resolution ConflictResolution movement.conflict_resolution (V1: lowest_id_wins only) max_steps int termination.max_steps The spread probability is a parameter of the hazard distribution. It is not evaluator randomness: it tells the model how likely spread is, but not which draws will succeed. Observation.to_dict() gives the serialised form, with the extra key observation_version. The action contract is unchanged: step(actions) needs exactly one action from allowed_actions for each active person. A move that cannot happen is legal and resolves to a blocked_* outcome. The observation does not contain: the seed, RNG state, stream seeds, future draws, scenario ID, description, content hash, schema version, or trapped. A change to the fields or the meaning of the observation MUST bump OBSERVATION_VERSION. Tests: tests/test_fairness.py.
