The tests check: the exact field lists of Observation, MapView and RulesView, and of the serialised form, that the object graph (walked through every instance attribute, not only the declared fields) holds only the public types above, and never a Scenario, Simulator, SimState, StepRecord, RunRecord, RNG or configuration object, that the seed, stream seeds, RNG positions and hidden metadata are absent from the observation and its JSON form, that observations are identical for different seeds and different hidden metadata, that two scenarios that differ only in one public rule give different observations, and that the rules are the only difference, that every RulesView value equals the scenario configuration. 5. Metrics input A metric MAY need both the Scenario and the RunRecord. The RunRecord has the actions, movements, ignitions, evacuations, casualties, trapped sets and states of each step. The static geometry (walls, exit positions, grid size) and the configuration (for example max_steps) are in the Scenario. The scenario_hash in the record binds the two together. Not every metric can be computed from a RunRecord alone. 6. Provenance and change control Every RunRecord header stores simulator_version, observation_version, schema_version, scenario_id, scenario_hash and seed. A new record always stores the active OBSERVATION_VERSION. verify_record rejects a record with a different simulator_version or observation_version, or a different scenario hash, with an explicit ReplayMismatchError. RunRecord.from_dict rejects a record that has no observation_version. A change that changes simulator output (any RunRecord byte) for the same scenario, seed and actions MUST bump SIMULATOR_VERSION. The golden digest test fails until the bump is made. A change to the observation fields or their meaning MUST bump OBSERVATION_VERSION. A change to the scenario file format MUST bump SCHEMA_VERSION. A documentation-only clarification of visibility does not need a bump. History. SIMULATOR_VERSION Change 0.1.0 Phase 1 deterministic core. 0.2.0 The RunRecord header gained observation_version. The dynamics did not change. With that key removed and the version set back to 0.1.0, every golden record hashes to its 0.1.0 digest. OBSERVATION_VERSION stays 1.0, because V1 was not released before this change.

title: Integrity & provenance
description: Validation, replay authentication and held-out evaluation.
text: Hidden-test integrity Field Value Modules emberbench.integrity, emberbench.leakguard Integrity protocol version 1.0 (INTEGRITY_PROTOCOL_VERSION) Benchmark revision 2 (BENCHMARK_REVISION); section 12 Pinned versions every key of benchmark_versions(): revision, simulator, interface, metrics, statistics, scoring, environment, generator, suite-definition and evaluation contracts (section 12) Runtime dependencies none (no cryptography library) The simulator, the public V1 suite and the generator are open source. A model can be tuned on all of them. A score is meaningful only on a held-out suite that no evaluated model has seen and that every model gets in exactly the same form. This document defines how an evaluator produces, uses and publishes such a suite, and what the published records prove. The protocol adds no new information to the model interface. An evaluated agent still receives only Observation (see model-interface.md). 1. Threat model Actor Trust What the protocol defends against Model submitter Not trusted Tuning on held-out scenarios or seeds; changing the model after seeing held-out material; claiming a result for another model version. Evaluator Trusted to keep private material private and to run the protocol Accidental leakage (committed files, packaged files, model inputs); accidental reuse of a different suite or manifest; silent repair of broken artifacts. Third-party reader Verifies published records Edited or mixed-up result, suite, manifest or version claims. Repository contributor Not trusted with held-out data Committing or packaging held-out material. Out of scope: a malicious evaluator, a compromised evaluator machine, a model that memorised scenarios from a leak outside the protocol, side channels in model-provider infrastructure, and proof of authorship (see section 12). 2. Asset classes emberbench.integrity.ASSET_POLICIES encodes this table. The repository and the Python package contain public development assets only. Class (AssetClass) Contents Release In repository / package Given to an agent public_development Simulator, generator code, public configs, the public V1 suite, docs, tests, test-only fixtures always yes yes (public scenarios reach a scored agent only as observations) private_heldout_suite Generator seed, rejection history, frozen generated suite, its batch ID and directory optional audit reveal after the batch is retired no no private_evaluation_manifest Evaluation manifest and its seeds; full per-model result artifacts, because they embed the manifest optional audit reveal after the batch is retired no no private_submission_metadata Submitted code, weights, endpoints, credentials, contact data never (only identity digests are published) no no public_provenance Provenance records, submission rosters, aggregate and paired statistics after evaluation no (published elsewhere) no Two facts follow from the existing formats: A full EvaluationResult artifact embeds the evaluation manifest, and so its seeds. Publish provenance and statistics after evaluation; publish full results only when the batch is retired. AggregateStatistics and PairedStatistics hold the manifest hash and the result digest, not the seeds. They are publishable after evaluation. No real hidden scenario, generator seed or scored evaluation seed is in the tests, fixtures, docs or package data. Tests use constants marked test-only. 3. Evaluation lifecycle Each step finishes before the next one starts. Generation finishes before any evaluated model sees the suite. The suite is never regenerated per model. # Step API Output 1 Freeze the benchmark revision a release with fixed benchmark_versions() versions to pin 2 Freeze each submitted model and code SubmissionIdentity, freeze_submission(identity, workspace) submission/identity.json 3 Generate the held-out suite from a private generator seed generate_suite(config, seed, batch_id=...) (or generate_post_submission_suite, section 8) in-memory suite 4 Freeze the generated suite freeze_generated_suite(generated, workspace / "generated-suite") generated-suite/ 5 Create the private paired evaluation manifest build_evaluation_manifest(suite, seeds), save_evaluation_manifest evaluation-manifest.json 6 Evaluate every model on the same frozen suite and manifest run_evaluation(suite, manifest, model_id, factory, path) result.json per model 7 Hash (and optionally sign) the provenance before any statistic is computed build_evaluation_provenance(...), external signer, save_provenance provenance.json 8 Publish allowed provenance and statistics aggregate_result, compare_results public records 9 Optionally reveal generation material for audit verify_regeneration / verify_post_submission_generation audit Use high-entropy seeds: secrets.randbits(256) for a generator seed and secrets.randbits(64) for each evaluation seed. Low-entropy seeds can be guessed, and the contamination scanner (section 9) cannot search for short values. build_evaluation_provenance refuses to pin an incomplete result, a public suite, a manifest that does not verify against the frozen suite, a result of another manifest, a result that fails authentication by replay, a submission whose label is not the result's model_id, and any artifact of another benchmark revision. 4. Evaluator workspace Private material lives in an evaluator-side directory outside the repository checkout. One workspace per evaluated model: evaluation-run/ submission/ identity.json SubmissionIdentity, written by freeze_submission ... the submitted material (not constrained) submission-roster.json only in post-submission mode generated-suite/ frozen generated suite: suite/ + generation.json evaluation-manifest.json result.json provenance.json workspace_stage(root) validates the layout and returns the WorkspaceStage reached: empty, submission_frozen, suite_frozen, manifest_frozen, evaluated, provenance_recorded. It raises IntegrityError if the workspace is inside an EMBERBench source checkout, holds an unexpected entry, or has a later artifact without an earlier one. Every model of one comparison has a byte-identical generated-suite/ and evaluation-manifest.json; their provenance records then pin equal suite and manifest hashes. verify_evaluation_workspace(root) loads every artifact from disk, verifies the frozen suite, authenticates the result by replay, and runs verify_evaluation_provenance with the identity in submission/identity.json pinned. Identity, roster and provenance files are written once; an existing file is never overwritten. 5. Provenance EvaluationProvenance is a versioned, immutable, public record of one model's evaluation. Its canonical form: { "integrity_protocol_version": "1.0", "versions": { "benchmark_revision": "2", "simulator": "0.2.0", "observation": "1.0", "action_schema": "1.0", "scenario_schema": "1.0", "metrics": "1.0", "crowd_diagnostics": "1.0", "statistics": "1.0", "generator": "1.1.0", "generator_config": "1.1", "generation_manifest": "1.1", "evaluation_manifest": "1.0", "evaluation_result": "1.0", "scoring": "1.0", "environment_pack": "1.0", "environment_world": "1.0", "family_rules": "1.0", "calibration_panel": "1.0", "difficulty_rules": "1.0", "admission_rules": "1.0", "composition": "1.0", "selection_rules": "1.0", "recipe_catalog": "1.0", "suite_freeze_record": "1.0" }, "protocol": {"mode": "shared_heldout_batch", "submission_roster_digest": null}, "suite": { "suite_id": "<batch ID>", "suite_version": "1.0.0", "suite_hash": "<64 hex>", "generation_hash": "<64 hex>", "generator_version": "1.1.0", "generator_config_hash": "<64 hex>", "scenario_count": 40 }, "evaluation_manifest": {"manifest_hash": "<64 hex>", "episode_count": 400}, "submission": { "identity": { "model_id": "model-a", "code_commit": "<40 hex>", "image_digest": null, "adapter_config_digest": "<64 hex>", "dependency_lock_digest": null }, "identity_digest": "<64 hex>" }, "evaluator": {"code_digest": null}, "result": {"result_digest": "<64 hex>", "result_version": "1.0", "episode_count": 400} } provenance_digest() is the SHA-256 of signing_payload(), the canonical JSON bytes of this object (sorted keys, no whitespace, ASCII). Equal content gives an equal digest on every platform; a one-bit change in any field changes it. There is no generator seed, no evaluation seed, no scenario content and no timestamp. A time is not part of the content identity; record it, if needed, in an external signed or timestamped envelope. suite.generation_hash pins the freeze record (config, batch ID, every scenario hash and proxy). suite.suite_hash pins the suite manifest. result.result_digest is the SHA-256 of the canonical result artifact. It equals the result_digest that aggregate_result and compare_results report, so published statistics link to the provenance. evaluator.code_digest is null unless the evaluator supplies it, for example with evaluator_code_digest() (SHA-256 of the installed emberbench/*.py files). The stored file is a ProvenanceRecord: {"provenance": {...}, "provenance_digest": "<64 hex>", "signing": "unsigned", "signatures": []} ProvenanceRecord.from_dict rejects unknown or missing fields at every level, wrong types, a digest that does not match, and a signing value that does not match the signature list. 6. Submission identity SubmissionIdentity is provider-neutral explicit metadata: Field Format Required model_id the label used in run_evaluation yes code_commit git commit SHA, 40 or 64 lowercase hex no image_digest sha256:<64 hex> container image digest no adapter_config_digest SHA-256 of the adapter or model config (digest_file, digest_directory) no dependency_lock_digest SHA-256 of the dependency lock file no A missing field is null. Nothing is inferred. pinned_fields lists the supplied digests; is_pinned is false for a bare label. These values identify content. They do not prove that this content is what ran, or who built it, unless an actual signature or trusted build process vouches for them. 7. Signatures Signing is optional and external. EMBERBench implements no cryptography and has no crypto dependency. Hashing works without signatures. A signature never changes provenance_digest. An external process signs provenance.signing_payload() and the evaluator records the result with record.with_signature(SignatureRecord(algorithm, key_id, signature_bytes)). The file stores the algorithm label, key ID and base64 signature bytes. An unsigned record says "signing": "unsigned". A signed record says "externally_signed". A file can never claim that a signature is valid. verify_evaluation_provenance(..., signature_verifier=f) calls f(signature, payload) for every signature. Only True accepts. Without a verifier, signatures are reported as signed_unverified and are not trusted. With require_signatures=True, an unsigned or unverified record is rejected. 8. Post-submission generation The strongest contamination-resistant mode. It makes it impossible for a submitter to change a model after held-out material exists: Freeze every submission's identity. Each must be pinned (at least one content digest). Freeze the roster: SubmissionRoster.of(identities), save_roster. Publish or escrow roster.roster_digest(). Only now choose the private seed (secrets.randbits(256)). Generate with generate_post_submission_suite(config, private_seed, roster, batch_id=...). The generator seed is SHA-256(domain, protocol version, private seed, roster digest), so the suite content depends on the frozen roster: no scenario of the batch can exist before every listed submission is frozen. Freeze the suite, then freeze the evaluation manifest, then evaluate. build_evaluation_provenance(..., roster=roster) records "mode": "post_submission_generation" and the roster digest. Verification needs the roster and checks that the submission is in it with this exact identity. After the batch is retired, reveal the private seed; verify_post_submission_generation(suite_dir, private_seed, roster) regenerates every byte. A submission changed after the roster was frozen gives another roster digest, another seed and a failed audit. No remote submission infrastructure is part of EMBERBench. 9. Contamination controls An evaluated agent receives only Observation (step, map, rules, people, burning cells, allowed actions). MODEL_VISIBLE_OBSERVATION_FIELDS lists exactly these fields, and Agent.act takes only the observation. The tests check that an agent never receives: the generator seed or the private seed, the evaluation seeds, the generation rejection history (it is never stored), the batch ID, the suite directory or path, scenario IDs or content hashes, the suite, generation, config or manifest hashes, provenance metadata or identity digests, prior hidden evaluation results or their digests. sensitive_tokens(frozen_suite, manifest, generator_seed=..., extra=...) and find_leaks(text, tokens) let an evaluator scan anything it sends to a model (for example a provider prompt built from a serialized observation). Values shorter than 8 characters are not scanned for. Limitations: a scanner finds only literal copies. It cannot detect a leaked scenario layout that was re-encoded, a model trained on a leaked batch, or a provider that logs prompts. The map, rules and people of each held-out scenario necessarily reach the model through observations; if the provider retains them, treat the batch as exposed after evaluation. 10. Leak guard emberbench.leakguard checks file paths, not file contents: Allowlist. Top-level entries: .github/, docs/, scenarios/, src/, tests/, tools/, .gitattributes, .gitignore, LICENSE, README.md, pyproject.toml. Under scenarios/ only scenarios/public/. Benchmark asset files (*.json) only under PUBLIC_ASSET_ROOTS: scenarios/public/ and tests/fixtures/. Forbidden components (case-insensitive, _ read as -): hidden, heldout, held-out, scored, private, secret(s), and names starting with hidden-, heldout-, held-out-, scored-, private-seed, private-eval, secret-manifest, production-eval, evaluation-run. Forbidden files: evaluator workspace and freeze-record names (generation.json, evaluation-manifest.json, submission-roster.json, identity.json, provenance.json, result.json) and seed or key types (.seed, .seeds, .key, .pem, .p12, .pfx). Wheel: only top-level emberbench/*.py, emberbench/py.typed and .dist-info metadata. Sdist: the repository rules plus setuptools metadata. tests/test_leakguard.py checks the checkout and builds a wheel and an sdist from a copy of the tracked files. CI also runs: python -m build --no-isolation --outdir dist . python tools/check_public_assets.py --dist dist Add --untracked to also check untracked, not ignored files before a commit. 11. Fail-closed verification verify_evaluation_provenance(record, frozen_suite=..., manifest=..., result=..., expected_submission=..., roster=..., expected_evaluator_code_digest=..., signature_verifier=..., require_signatures=...) re-derives every pin from the actual artifacts and raises IntegrityError on: a wrong suite hash, generation hash, config hash or scenario count, a wrong evaluation manifest hash, or a manifest that does not verify against the frozen suite, a wrong result digest, a result of another manifest, an incomplete result, or a result that fails authentication by replay, any version that differs from this benchmark revision, a submission identity that differs from the pinned one (when pinned), or a label that is not the result's model_id, an evaluator code digest that differs or is missing (when pinned), a missing or wrong roster in post-submission mode, or a roster in shared mode, a public suite or any other incompatible artifact, malformed, missing or unknown fields at any level, a signature the verifier rejects, or missing or unverified signatures when they are required. Nothing is repaired, skipped or re-derived into the record. 12. Benchmark revision policy A benchmark revision (BENCHMARK_REVISION) defines what a score means. The benchmark revision changes when a released contract changes incompatibly and that contract defines one of these: the meaning of a score, the identity of an environment (the world an agent is evaluated in), the composition or admission of a suite (which worlds are selected and evaluated), the semantics of the generator, the evaluator protocol. Bump the revision, together with the component version, for: a simulator semantic change (SIMULATOR_VERSION), an observation or action schema change (OBSERVATION_VERSION, ACTION_SCHEMA_VERSION, SCHEMA_VERSION), a metric or statistic definition change (METRICS_VERSION, STATISTICS_VERSION, CROWD_DIAGNOSTICS_VERSION), a change to the EMBER Score formula, its constants, its arithmetic or its serialization (SCORING_VERSION), an environment identity change (ENVIRONMENT_PACK_VERSION, ENVIRONMENT_WORLD_VERSION), a generator semantics or config format change (GENERATOR_VERSION, GENERATOR_CONFIG_VERSION, GENERATION_MANIFEST_VERSION), a change to the suite-definition rules: family rules (FAMILY_RULES_VERSION), the calibration panel, difficulty or admission rules (CALIBRATION_PANEL_VERSION, DIFFICULTY_RULES_VERSION, ADMISSION_RULES_VERSION), composition, selection, the recipe catalog or the suite freeze record (COMPOSITION_VERSION, SELECTION_RULES_VERSION, RECIPE_CATALOG_VERSION, SUITE_FREEZE_RECORD_VERSION), an evaluation manifest or result format change (EVALUATION_MANIFEST_VERSION, EVALUATION_RESULT_VERSION), discovered held-out leakage that the current protocol permits, an invalid evaluation protocol, a material bug that affects ranking or comparison. benchmark_versions() pins every one of these versions, and each value is the owning module's constant. Evaluation provenance records all of them. verify_evaluation_provenance fails closed when any recorded value differs from the running benchmark, or when a key is missing or unknown. Examples: Change Revision A new private suite, generated under the identical revision and rules Same revision New evaluator-private seeds (generator or evaluation) under unchanged rules Same revision Changed family, calibration-panel, difficulty, admission, composition or selection rules New revision Changed scoring formula or scoring constants New revision Changed generator semantics or config format New revision Scores from different revisions are never compared. Provenance of another revision fails verification. Revision history. Revision Content 1 First integrity protocol. Never released as a scored benchmark. 2 The official EMBER Score (SCORING_VERSION 1.0) and environment packs, and the generator 1.1 suite-definition contracts (family rules, calibration, admission, composition and selection, all 1.0). These changes came between two releases, so one pre-release step covers them. A regenerated held-out batch under the same revision is different: new private seed, new batch ID, new frozen suite and new manifest, with the same code and versions. Use it when a batch is exposed (provider retention, a leak, a reveal for audit) or retired on schedule. Rules: Never replace a compromised batch silently. Announce it, keep its provenance, and mark its results as compromised. Results on different batches are separate comparisons. Every model in one comparison is evaluated on one batch and one manifest. A protocol flaw that let leakage happen is a revision change, not just a new batch. 13. What EMBERBench cannot prove Hashes establish content identity and integrity, not authorship. A matching digest shows that two artifacts are byte-identical, not who made them or when. A SubmissionIdentity names content. It does not prove that the named code produced the actions, unless a trusted build or signature process stands behind the evaluation. An unverified signature proves nothing. EMBERBench never checks a signature itself. The evaluator is trusted. A malicious evaluator can leak a batch, choose a favourable seed, or run another model; the protocol makes these harder to hide, not impossible. Without an external timestamp, records do not prove when a step happened. Post-submission generation proves an order only through the roster digest and the later seed reveal. A clean scan for sensitive tokens does not prove that a model never saw held-out material elsewhere.

title: Reference agents
description: Hand-coded agents and planning references.
text: Reference baselines (baselines version 1.0) Reference baselines are anchors, not benchmark winners. EMBERBench ships five deterministic, non-LLM reference agents. They make benchmark results readable: a model that does no better than static-shortest-path-v1 on a scenario family has not shown more than a textbook routing rule. The baselines are not tuned to win, and no result here is a leaderboard entry or a ranking. Their EMBER Scores (scoring.md) are reference anchors, not entries. The module is emberbench.baselines. A separate, privileged upper-bound analysis is in emberbench.oracle (section 5). It is not a baseline and not a model. 1. The fair-baseline contract Every registered baseline is a fair model. It uses the public model interface only (model-interface.md): A zero-argument AgentFactory builds a new agent for every episode. The agent is built from its public baseline configuration only. act(observation) receives one Observation and returns one action for every active person. It never receives the scenario, the evaluator seed, the EvaluationManifest, a RunRecord, SimState, RNG state, future fire, the scenario ID or hash, or generation metadata. Every decision is a pure function of the observation and the configuration. No baseline keeps state between steps. No baseline reads the clock, the OS, environment variables, the random module or any simulator RNG. No output depends on hash order, dict insertion order or the order of people in the observation. Baselines run through the normal evaluation path with no special case: from emberbench import agent_policy_factory, baseline_factory, run_evaluation factory = baseline_factory("fire-aware-shortest-path-v1") result = run_evaluation(suite, manifest, "fire-aware-shortest-path-v1", agent_policy_factory(factory), "fire-aware.json") Use the same EvaluationManifest for every baseline and every model, so the results pair exactly (evaluation.md). 2. Registry ID Version Config Description random-legal-v1 1.0 {"seed": 0} Uniform seeded choice among stay and moves into in-bounds non-wall cells. nearest-exit-greedy-v1 1.0 {} Beeline (Manhattan) toward the exit with the shortest wall-only path; ignores fire and people. static-shortest-path-v1 1.0 {} Shortest wall-only path to the nearest exit, replanned each step; ignores fire and people. fire-aware-shortest-path-v1 1.0 {} Shortest path avoiding currently burning cells and exits; flees the fire if no safe route exists. congestion-aware-v1 1.0 {} Fire-aware shortest paths with exits assigned by current load (one person per exit per step). The registry is a fixed, read-only table (emberbench.baselines.BASELINES). Nothing is imported or instantiated from a string. get_baseline(baseline_id) returns a BaselineSpec. An unknown ID (or a value that is not a string) raises BaselineError. There is no fuzzy match and no default. baseline_factory(baseline_id, config=None) returns a zero-argument factory. config is the baseline's config object, its to_dict() form (parsed strictly: exact keys, exact types, ranges) or None for the default. A config of the wrong type raises BaselineError. BaselineSpec.descriptor(config) is the canonical description: baselines_version, baseline_id, baseline_version, privileged (always false here) and config. BaselineSpec.config_digest(config) is the SHA-256 of the canonical JSON of the descriptor. Record it next to the model_id when you publish a baseline result. The default digests are pinned in tests/test_baselines.py. model_id in run_evaluation stays a free-text label. A baseline run with a non-default config should use a label that says so, for example random-legal-v1+seed=7. 3. Shared conventions Distance. Breadth-first search over 4-neighbours, one BFS per exit, from the observation's static map. "Wall-only" means walls block and nothing else does. Move order. Moves are tried in the order of observation.allowed_actions without stay: north, south, east, west in V1. The first move that meets the rule wins. This is how equal shortest paths are broken: the path is the one whose next move comes first in that order. Equal exits. The exit with the lowest exit ID (plain string order) wins. Burning cells. V1 rules R5 and R6: a burning exit never evacuates, and a move into a burning cell is refused (blocked) or fatal (casualty). The fire-aware baselines therefore treat every currently burning cell as impassable and every currently burning exit as unusable, under both enter_fire policies. Fallback (fire-aware and congestion-aware). When a person has no currently safe route to any usable exit, the person flees: among stay and every move into an in-bounds, non-wall, non-burning cell, it takes the one with the largest wall-only distance to the nearest burning cell. Ties go to stay, then to the move order. Complexity is per step. N is the number of grid cells, E the number of exits and P the number of active people. 4. The baselines random-legal-v1 Visible information: map walls and size, allowed_actions, each active person's ID and position, the step number. Algorithm: the legal set of a person is stay plus every move into an in-bounds, non-wall cell, in allowed_actions order. One element is chosen uniformly. Randomness: no evaluator randomness. The draw is SHA-256 of the canonical JSON of ["emberbench/baseline/random-legal/1", seed, step, person_id, counter]. The first 8 bytes are a 64-bit word. Words at or above the largest multiple of the set size are rejected (the counter goes up), so the choice is exactly uniform. seed is a public baseline parameter in [0, 2**64 - 1] (default 0). It is model configuration, not an evaluator seed, and its domain label differs from every simulator stream label. The same observation and config always give the same actions. Different people and steps get independent draws. Tie-breaking: none needed. Complexity: O(P). Each draw needs about one hash. Known weakness: it does not try to leave. It ignores exits, fire and people. It anchors the floor of the scale. Fair or privileged: fair. nearest-exit-greedy-v1 Visible information: map walls, size and exits; active people. Algorithm: the target is the exit with the shortest wall-only path from the person. The person then takes the first move into an in-bounds, non-wall cell that lowers the straight-line (Manhattan) distance to that exit. If no move does, the person stays. Tie-breaking: equal exits by exit ID; equal moves by move order. Complexity: O(E * N + P * E). Known weakness (intentional): it is a beeline. It stalls for good when a wall lies between the person and the exit (it scores 0 on v1-pub-08-maze-deceptive-exit). It ignores fire and people. Interpretation note: the exit is chosen by wall-only path distance, but each step only has to lower the straight-line distance. If each step had to lower the path distance, this baseline would be identical to static-shortest-path-v1. Fair or privileged: fair. static-shortest-path-v1 Visible information: map walls, size and exits; active people. Algorithm: one BFS per exit over non-wall cells. The target is the exit with the shortest path from the person's current position. The person takes a move that lowers that distance by one. It replans from the observed position every step. Fire, burning exits and other people are ignored. A person with no wall-only route to any exit stays. Tie-breaking: equal exits by exit ID; equal shortest paths and equal actions by move order. Complexity: O(E * N + P * E). Known weakness: it walks into fire and toward burning exits, and it sends every person to the same nearest exit, whatever the queue. Fair or privileged: fair. fire-aware-shortest-path-v1 Visible information: as above, plus the currently burning cells. Algorithm: like static-shortest-path-v1, but every currently burning cell is impassable and every currently burning exit is unusable. It recomputes from each observation. It never predicts future spread, and it never uses the evaluator seed or the spread probability. With no currently safe route the person uses the flee fallback. Tie-breaking: as static-shortest-path-v1; the fallback as in section 3. Complexity: O(E * N + P * E), plus O(N) for the fallback map when at least one person needs it. Known weakness: a route that is safe now can burn before the person passes. It reacts only after the fire blocks a route, and it ignores congestion. Fair or privileged: fair. congestion-aware-v1 Visible information: map, currently burning cells, and the current positions of all active people. It does not use CrowdDiagnostics, which are evaluator-side and never reach a model. Algorithm: The fire-aware distance fields, one per usable exit. People with a safe route are sorted by their nearest-exit distance, then by person ID. In that order, each person takes the exit with the lowest estimated evacuation step max(distance, load + 1), where load is the number of people already assigned to that exit. An exit lets one person through per step (V1 rule R4), so this is the earliest step that exit could take the person if everyone ahead used it. The person takes a move that lowers the distance to the assigned exit by one. A move into a cell that no active person occupies now is preferred. People with no safe route use the flee fallback. Tie-breaking: equal estimates go to the shorter distance, then to the lowest exit ID; equal moves to a free cell first, then by move order. Complexity: O(E * N + P log P + P * E). Known weakness: the load is a snapshot count, not a forecast. People can switch exits from one step to the next as the counts change. It does not plan around other people's paths, and it is not a model of human crowd behaviour. Fair or privileged: fair. 5. The privileged escape bound (not a baseline) emberbench.oracle is privileged. It reads the Scenario and the evaluator seed, and therefore the whole future fire. It is an upper-bound reference analysis. It is not an agent: it has no act method, it is not in the registry, it is not exported from the top-level package, and it produces no actions and no EvaluationResult. Its numbers must never be shown as a model competitor. Why it is correct. In V1 the fire never sees people or actions (emberbench.fire). Under one scenario and seed, the burning set at every step is the same for every policy. fire_trajectory(scenario, seed) reproduces that set from the fire model and the seed-derived fire stream. A test checks it against the simulator on every public scenario. For each person alone, a time-expanded BFS over (cell, step) finds the earliest step at which the person can reach a usable exit. It follows the simulator's phase order: a move into a cell that burns at the start of the step is never useful, an exit that is not burning at the start of the step evacuates at once, and a person on a cell that burns after fire spread is a casualty. Other people can only block moves (rules R1-R4), so ignoring them is a relaxation. Hence, for every policy and every episode: max_evacuated (people who can escape alone) is an upper bound on safety.evacuated, min_person_time_to_safety_total is a lower bound on time.person_time_to_safety_total, and each evacuated person's step is at least that person's bound. The tests check these three facts for every baseline on the development manifest. The bound is tight for a single person. With crowds it is usually not attainable, because people compete for exits. It says nothing about casualties versus stranded people. Cost. O(T * N) per person, where T is max_steps. from emberbench.oracle import privileged_manifest_bounds # privileged: evaluator-side only bounds = privileged_manifest_bounds(suite, manifest) A full multi-person oracle (a joint plan with the known fire) is not included. An optimal joint plan is a combinatorial multi-agent search, and a prioritized planner is not an upper bound, so it would be a misleading "oracle". 6. Development results Public V1 suite, development seeds (0, 1, 2) (manifest hash 7b9aae45e5e2828f881b2f14d8e5585627e5f8bdbb137a1ed2331bf10ce8c876), 30 episodes, 561 person-episodes. These are development numbers for orientation only. They are not scored results, and the order between baselines can differ on other scenarios. always-stay is a test control, not a registered baseline. Model Evacuated Casualties Stranded Person-time to safety always-stay (control) 0 555 6 80310 random-legal-v1 12 546 3 78540 nearest-exit-greedy-v1 404 148 9 31358 static-shortest-path-v1 419 142 0 29933 fire-aware-shortest-path-v1 433 128 0 29084 congestion-aware-v1 526 35 0 14960 privileged escape bound ≤ 561 – – ≥ 5432 Evacuated people per scenario (sum over the three seeds): Scenario People stay random greedy static fire-aware congestion bound v1-pub-01-single-exit-sparse 12 0 0 12 12 12 12 12 v1-pub-02-single-exit-dense 108 0 3 81 81 81 102 108 v1-pub-03-corridor-bottleneck 24 0 0 21 21 21 24 24 v1-pub-04-unequal-exits 15 0 0 15 15 15 15 15 v1-pub-05-central-ignition 24 0 0 18 18 18 18 24 v1-pub-06-threatened-exit 18 0 0 9 9 15 15 18 v1-pub-07-multiple-ignitions 27 0 0 21 21 21 24 27 v1-pub-08-maze-deceptive-exit 15 0 0 0 15 15 15 15 v1-pub-09-crowd-100-split-flow 300 0 9 216 216 219 285 300 v1-pub-10-route-invalidation 18 0 0 11 11 16 16 18 How to read this: Every person is escapable alone in every development episode (the bound is 561 of 561). Every loss is a matter of routing, fire timing and coordination, not of an impossible start. Fire awareness matters where the fire threatens a route or an exit (threatened-exit, route-invalidation). Exit load matters in dense and crowded scenarios. Even the best baseline leaves a gap to the bound in person-time to safety (14960 against at least 5432). On the single-exit scenarios, congestion-aware-v1 gains from its free-cell move preference, not from exit choice. The tests do not pin this table. They pin only broad, robust facts (section 7), plus exact digests of the baseline runs on a smaller development manifest. 7. What the tests prove tests/test_baselines.py: Registry: the five IDs, versions, descriptions and descriptors; pinned config digests; a read-only registry; unknown IDs and invalid configs fail closed. Integration: every baseline runs unchanged through run_evaluation(..., agent_policy_factory(...)) on one shared manifest, including the canonical sparse, corridor-bottleneck, 100-person and stochastic route-invalidation scenarios, and a generated suite. Leakage: the factory is called with no arguments; act gets exactly one Observation and nothing else; the evaluator seed, the manifest hash and the scenario ID never occur in it; the same observation gives the same actions under four different evaluator seeds; the module imports no scenario, manifest, run-record, simulator, state, RNG, fire, generator, crowd-diagnostics or oracle API (an AST check plus a check of the module namespace). Determinism: a repeated run gives a byte-identical artifact; reversing the action dict's insertion order gives a byte-identical artifact; reordering people and burning cells in the observation gives the same actions; three PYTHONHASHSEED values in fresh processes give identical outputs; golden digests of all runs and golden two-step action traces are pinned, and CI checks them on Linux, Windows and macOS with Python 3.12 and 3.13. Sanity (no total ranking): the shortest-path baselines evacuate more than always-stay; fire-aware avoids a currently burning route that static takes; congestion-aware lowers person-time and the largest exit share in a designed door bottleneck; greedy stalls behind a wall that static goes around; the random baseline is deterministic for its seed and changes with it. Privileged bound: it is separated from the fair interface; its fire trajectory matches the simulator; it holds for every baseline and episode; it is tight for one person and finds a person who cannot escape. 8. Versioning BASELINES_VERSION = "1.0" is independent of every other version. Bump it when any baseline can act differently for the same observation and configuration, or when the registry or config format changes. A baseline's own baseline_version (and its -vN ID suffix) changes when that baseline's algorithm changes. This phase changes no other version: SIMULATOR_VERSION, OBSERVATION_VERSION, ACTION_SCHEMA_VERSION, SCHEMA_VERSION, METRICS_VERSION, STATISTICS_VERSION and the suite formats are unchanged, and all public scenario and suite hashes are unchanged.

title: Statistical analysis
description: Intervals, resampling and paired comparisons.
text: Aggregate and paired statistics (statistics version 1.0) This document defines the statistical summaries that EMBERBench computes over evaluation results. The code is in src/emberbench/statistics.py. The tests are in tests/test_statistics.py. There is no EMBER score or global winner in this module. (The EMBER Score is a separate module: see scoring.md.) This module does not rank models, combine metrics or produce a leaderboard. Every number belongs to one named metric. Win/loss/tie counts exist per metric only. Out of scope here: leaderboards, a composite score, model rankings, provider adapters, procedural generation and a CLI. 1. Entry points from emberbench import aggregate_result, compare_results, load_evaluation_result, load_suite suite = load_suite("scenarios/public/v1") a = load_evaluation_result("results/model-a.json", suite) b = load_evaluation_result("results/model-b.json", suite) stats_a = aggregate_result(a, suite) # one model paired = compare_results(a, b, suite) # A - B, per metric print(stats_a.digest(), paired.digest()) Function Returns Artifact field artifact aggregate_result(result, suite, *, resamples=2000) AggregateStatistics "aggregate" compare_results(a, b, suite, *, resamples=2000) PairedStatistics "paired" Both artifacts are immutable dataclasses with to_dict(), to_json() (canonical JSON) and digest() (SHA-256 of the canonical JSON). They carry statistics_version = "1.0". This version is separate from SIMULATOR_VERSION, OBSERVATION_VERSION, SCHEMA_VERSION, METRICS_VERSION and the evaluation artifact versions, which this module does not change. Bump STATISTICS_VERSION when any statistic, its serialization or the bootstrap stream changes. 2. Fail-closed input An EvaluationResult in memory is not trusted as given. Before any episode is used, both functions: rebuild the evaluation manifest from its dictionary and require that it is equal to the original; call verify_manifest(manifest, suite): the suite ID, version and hash and the simulator, observation and metrics versions must match the running code; rebuild the EvaluationResult, which repeats its structural checks (manifest order, no duplicates, every episode equal to its manifest entry, record headers equal to the manifest); for every episode: resolve its scenario from the suite by ID and content hash, recompute EpisodeMetrics from the run record (this authenticates the record by simulator replay), and require that the stored metrics equal the recomputed metrics exactly (canonical JSON). Any failure raises StatisticsInputError (a subclass of EvaluationError). Nothing is repaired, skipped or partly summarized. compare_results first calls pair_results(a, b). Results from different evaluation manifests raise EvaluationError before any replay. 3. Supported metrics and directions Each metric is a per-episode scalar from EpisodeMetrics. The module rebuilds it as an exact Fraction from the integer counts in the metrics (see §10) and requires that the float of that fraction equals the stored value. Metric Source field Kind Direction Exact definition (per episode) Undefined when evacuated_rate safety.evacuated_rate outcome higher is better evacuated / population never casualty_rate safety.casualty_rate outcome lower is better casualties / population never stranded_rate safety.stranded_rate outcome lower is better stranded / population never terminal_trapped_rate safety.terminal_trapped_rate outcome lower is better terminal_trapped_count / population never mean_person_time_to_safety time.mean_person_time_to_safety outcome lower is better person_time_to_safety_total / population never blocked_rate movement.blocked_rate behaviour lower is better blocked_moves / movement_attempts no movement attempts congestion_block_rate movement.congestion_block_rate behaviour lower is better congestion_blocks / movement_attempts no movement attempts aggregate_path_efficiency path_efficiency.aggregate_path_efficiency proxy higher is better total_static_lower_bound / total_cells_moved no measured movement mean_exposure fire_exposure.mean_exposure proxy lower is better (Σ_d count_d / d) / active_person_states never exits_used exits.exits_used descriptive none number of exits with n_e >= 1 never max_exit_share exits.max_exit_share descriptive none max_e n_e / E E = 0 exit_balance exits.exit_balance descriptive none normalized Gini-Simpson index K = 1 or E = 0 The per-episode definitions are in metrics.md. Notes: Kinds. Outcome metrics are terminal safety and time results. Behaviour metrics describe observed movement. Proxy metrics approximate a quantity that is not measured directly (path optimality, fire danger). Descriptive metrics describe the run and are not objectives. Directions are used only to read the sign of a paired difference (§8). They do not make a metric an objective by itself. mean_person_time_to_safety counts every non-evacuee at max_steps (censoring), so it mixes speed and safety. Read it with the safety rates. blocked_rate and congestion_block_rate are lower-is-better per metric, but a run can lower them by not moving. Never read them alone. Exit metrics have no direction. Equal exit use is often not optimal (one exit can be much closer, or threatened by fire). exit_balance is never an objective, and no win/loss/tie count exists for any exit metric. 4. Groups: overall, per scenario, per family Each artifact holds the same summaries for three kinds of group: Group Episodes Order overall every scheduled episode — scenarios every scheduled episode of one scenario suite manifest order families every scheduled episode of every scenario in the family ScenarioFamily declaration order A scenario with several families contributes all of its episodes to every one of those families. Family views can therefore overlap, and the family counts do not add up to the overall counts. A family with no scheduled scenario is not listed. Overall statistics use the episode observations directly. They are never an average of scenario or family means. With unequal group sizes (for example after missing episodes) the two are different, and only the episode-level value is reported. Each episode has equal weight; a scenario with more scheduled seeds has more weight in overall. 5. Descriptive statistics For one metric in one group, let x_1, …, x_n be the defined values of the observed episodes, and x_(1) <= … <= x_(n) the same values in ascending order. Field Formula Defined when n number of defined values always mean (Σ_i x_i) / n n >= 1 median the type-7 quantile at p = 1/2 (the mean of the two middle values when n is even) n >= 1 variance sample variance Σ_i (x_i - mean)² / (n - 1) n >= 2 std sqrt(variance) n >= 2 min, max x_(1), x_(n) n >= 1 quantiles type-7 quantiles at p25, p50, p75, p90, p95 n >= 1 An undefined statistic is null (None). It is never 0. Quantile rule (Hyndman-Fan type 7) With 0-based sorted values y[0] <= … <= y[n-1] and a level p in [0, 1]: h = (n - 1) · p j = floor(h) g = h - j Q(p) = y[j] + g · (y[j+1] - y[j]) (Q(p) = y[j] when g = 0) This is the default of R (type = 7) and of NumPy (method = "linear"). The levels are fixed: p25 = 1/4, p50 = 1/2, p75 = 3/4, p90 = 9/10, p95 = 19/20. With n = 1 every quantile is the single value. Example: for 1, 2, 3, 4 the quantiles are p25 = 1.75, p50 = 2.5, p75 = 3.25, p90 = 3.7, p95 = 3.85, and the sample variance is 5/3. 6. Robustness and completeness counts Each aggregate group has a robustness object of raw episode counts. There are no rates here, so nothing hides the denominators. Field Counts episodes … scheduled in the manifest for this group observed with an authenticated result missing scheduled, with no result (scheduled - observed) all_resolved observed, terminated with all_resolved max_steps observed, terminated at the step limit with_casualties observed, casualties > 0 with_stranded observed, stranded > 0 zero_evacuation observed, evacuated = 0 all_resolved + max_steps = observed. An episode can count in several of the last four rows. 7. Missing and undefined data There are two different kinds of absent value. Both are reported; neither is imputed. Missing episode. The manifest schedules it but the result has no entry for it (for example, an interrupted run). It is missing, not a model failure: it is not counted as a casualty, a timeout or zero evacuation. The artifact lists every missing episode key (missing_episodes), and every group gives missing_indices and robustness.missing. Undefined metric. The episode has a result, but the metric is None for it (for example blocked_rate when nobody tried to move). The per-metric summary counts it in undefined. For each metric summary: scheduled = observed + missing n = observed - undefined The statistics use the n defined values only. No value is filled in with zero, a mean, a worst case or a value from another episode. 8. Paired comparison compare_results(a, b, suite) uses pair_results(a, b) for the exact episode join. An episode is paired only when both results contain the same key (manifest hash, index, scenario ID, scenario hash, seed). Unpaired episodes are never compared; they are listed in missing_from_a and missing_from_b. For one metric in one group, with paired episodes k where the metric is defined for both A and B: delta_k = value_A(k) - value_B(k) (always A - B) Each PairedMetricComparison reports: Field Meaning paired paired episodes in the group missing_from_a, missing_from_b scheduled episodes in the group that A or B does not have undefined paired episodes where the metric is None for A or for B deltas every (episode index, delta_k), in manifest order statistics §5 statistics of the deltas: mean, median, std, quantiles, … (n = paired - undefined) mean_delta_ci §9 interval for the mean delta delta_positive, delta_negative, delta_zero counts of delta > 0, < 0, = 0 a_better, b_better, ties win/loss/tie counts by the metric's direction Win/loss/tie, per metric: Direction a_better b_better ties higher is better delta > 0 delta < 0 delta = 0 lower is better delta < 0 delta > 0 delta = 0 descriptive null null null There is no count across metrics, no majority vote and no composite. Swapping A and B negates every delta and swaps a_better and b_better. 9. Confidence intervals Each metric summary has mean_ci (aggregate) or mean_delta_ci (paired): a 95 % percentile bootstrap interval for the mean. Let x_1, …, x_n be the defined values (aggregate) or the paired deltas (paired). If n < 5 the interval is null. For each of R resamples, draw n indices uniformly with replacement from 0 … n-1 and take the mean of the selected values. In a paired comparison the resampling unit is the paired episode, so A and B stay together in the delta. Sort the R resample means. The bounds are their type-7 quantiles at 0.025 and 0.975. R is resamples: the default is 2000; any integer in [100, 1 000 000] is accepted. All means are exact fractions; only the bounds become floats. Determinism. The bootstrap never uses random, the time or OS entropy. Its stream seed is seed = SHA-256( canonical JSON of { statistics_version, purpose ("aggregate_mean" or "paired_mean_delta"), evaluation_manifest_hash, result_digests, group [kind, name], metric, resamples } ) where each result digest is the SHA-256 of the canonical EvaluationResult (the artifact as saved). The 64-bit words come from SHAKE-256 in counter mode: block k is SHAKE-256("emberbench/statistics/bootstrap/v1\0" || seed || k) (k as 8 big-endian bytes), read as 512 big-endian unsigned 64-bit words. An index below n is drawn by rejection sampling (word < 2^64 - 2^64 mod n, then word mod n), so there is no modulo bias. The seed is in the output for audit. Identical inputs give identical intervals on every platform. Different data, labels or manifests give different streams. This stream shares nothing with the simulator's SplitMix64 streams. Interpretation. An interval describes the uncertainty of the mean over this evaluation sample of scenarios and seeds, resampled at the episode level. It does not prove that one model is better in general, on other scenarios or on other seeds. Episodes of one scenario are not independent of each other, and the public suite is small, so treat intervals as descriptive. 10. Exact arithmetic and serialization Per-episode values are exact Fractions rebuilt from integer counts (for mean_exposure, from the fire-distance histogram: Σ count_d / d). Means, medians, variances, quantiles, min/max, deltas and bootstrap means are exact Fractions in the dataclasses. The output boundary is to_dict(): each exact value becomes its correctly rounded float. The standard deviation is the one irrational value: it is math.sqrt(float(variance)), which IEEE 754 rounds correctly. Every list is in manifest, suite or ScenarioFamily order. No result depends on dict or set iteration order or on PYTHONHASHSEED. to_json() is canonical JSON (sorted keys, no whitespace, ASCII, no NaN). digest() is its SHA-256. The model ID label, the input result digests and resamples are part of the artifact, so a change to any of them changes the digest. 11. Artifact layout AggregateStatistics.to_dict(): statistics_version, artifact = "aggregate", model_id, evaluation_manifest_hash, suite_id, suite_version, suite_hash, simulator_version, observation_version, metrics_version, result_digest, scheduled_episodes, observed_episodes, missing_episodes[], metric_definitions[], methods{quantiles, variance, std, bootstrap}, overall{kind, name, episode_indices, missing_indices, robustness, metrics[]}, scenarios[], families[] Each metrics[] entry: metric, scheduled, observed, missing, undefined, statistics{n, mean, median, variance, std, min, max, quantiles{p25…p95}}, mean_ci{method, statistic, level, resamples, seed, lower, upper} | null. PairedStatistics.to_dict() has the same header with model_a, model_b, result_digest_a, result_digest_b, delta = "A - B", paired_count, missing_from_a[], missing_from_b[], and groups with paired_indices, missing_from_a, missing_from_b and the §8 fields per metric. 12. Summary of what each section is Concept Where Is it a judgement? Descriptive statistics §5, statistics no: a summary of observed values Robustness counts §6, robustness no: raw episode counts Missing / undefined §7 no: completeness accounting Paired differences §8, deltas no: signed A - B values Per-metric win/loss/tie §8 per metric only, by its direction Metrics with no direction §3, exit metrics never a winner Confidence intervals §9 uncertainty over this sample only There is no EMBER score or global winner in this module.

title: Benchmark methodology
description: The scientific rationale behind the benchmark.
text: EMBERBench scientific evaluation methodology This document explains why the EMBER Score (scoring version 1.0) has its form. The normative definition is scoring.md. The frozen environment protocol is environment-pack.md. The full output of the sensitivity study is scoring-study-results.md. Nothing here changes the simulator, the observation, the schemas or the metrics. The score is computed only from authenticated, replayed run records. 1. Summary of decisions Question Decision Form EMBER = 100 * Safety * Quality^beta * Severity; every factor in [0, 1] (design F of section 5.9) Safety E^2 * P_casualty * P_stranding, with a discrete incident factor plus a rate term for each loss type, and a catastrophic gate at half the savable people Attribution per person: a loss is avoidable when that person's privileged earliest escape exists; unavoidable losses are never transferred between people Quality weighted geometric mean of Time, Hazard, Path and Replanning (weights 3/8, 2/8, 1/8, 2/8), raised to the derived exponent beta = ln 0.6 / ln 0.5 Trajectory invariance every score input is a function of the authenticated state trajectory; identical trajectories score identically (R16) Congestion not a score input; block rate, contested cells, hotspots and exit throughput are mandatory report diagnostics; a bottleneck is charged by its realized delay (Time against the cut-capacity bound Q_cut), exposure and losses (section 5.12) Severe failures per quality component, a threshold in natural units; each severe component multiplies the score by 0.8 * (q / q_severe) Normalization each quality component is a privileged relaxed optimum divided by the actual value, so it is relative to the difficulty of that exact episode Failures missing, invalid output, model error and timeout score 0 and stay in every mean Aggregation episode (mean over trials) -> scenario -> primary family -> overall, each an unweighted mean Uncertainty stratified two-stage percentile bootstrap, 95% Comparison paired; four outcomes; "better" needs the interval to exclude 0 and a difference of at least 1 point Leaderboard score to 0.1, then safety-first tie-breaks; separate from significance Environment one frozen environment pack per evaluation, identical for every model 2. Literature Each source below is a primary source. The right column says what EMBERBench takes from it. Source Relevant finding Use in EMBERBench Mattson et al., MLPerf Training Benchmark, MLSys 2020, arXiv:1910.01500 A result counts only when the model reaches a fixed quality target; time-to-train is measured only after that gate; closed division rules fix the environment; multiple runs are required because of run-to-run variance. Safety acts as a gate and a multiplier, not as one more additive term. Fixed environment (pack). Repeated trials for stochastic models. Reddi et al., MLPerf Inference Benchmark, ISCA 2020, arXiv:1911.02549 Scenarios have fixed quality targets and latency bounds; results that miss the target are invalid, not "partially scored". Invalid output and timeouts score 0 and are never dropped. Cost and latency are reported separately from quality. Liang et al., Holistic Evaluation of Language Models (HELM), TMLR 2023, arXiv:2211.09110 A single number hides trade-offs; report many metrics side by side under standardized conditions; aggregate with explicit, documented rules. The headline ships with every component, family score, tail statistic and coverage count. Operational metrics are separate. Cobbe et al., Leveraging Procedural Generation to Benchmark RL (Procgen), ICML 2020, arXiv:1912.01588 Normalize each environment's return with per-environment constants so environments are comparable; evaluate generalization on held-out levels. Each component is normalized per episode by a privileged reference. Held-out generated suites in packs. Bellemare et al., The Arcade Learning Environment, JAIR 2013; Mnih et al., Human-level control through deep RL, Nature 2015 Human-normalized score (agent - random) / (human - random); aggregate across games after normalization. Baseline/oracle normalization was considered (section 5.6); the privileged optimum is used as the upper reference instead of a human. Machado et al., Revisiting the Arcade Learning Environment, JAIR 2018, arXiv:1709.06009 Evaluation protocols must be fixed and reported (stochasticity, episode termination, number of runs); the median of normalized scores is more robust than the mean. Fixed pack and stochasticity protocol. Median and lower-tail statistics reported next to the mean. Ray, Achiam and Amodei, Benchmarking Safe Exploration in Deep RL (Safety Gym), OpenAI 2019 Report task return and constraint cost separately; a policy that violates constraints is not "better" because of a higher return. Safety is separate from quality and multiplies it; a loss can never be bought back by speed beyond the documented bound. Ji et al., Safety-Gymnasium, NeurIPS 2023 Datasets and Benchmarks, arXiv:2310.12567 Unified safe-RL benchmark; reward and cost are reported together; safety is evaluated per task. Per-family reporting of the Safety factor. Altman, Constrained Markov Decision Processes, 1999; Achiam et al., Constrained Policy Optimization, ICML 2017, arXiv:1705.10528 Safety as a constraint, not as a weighted reward term; constraint satisfaction comes before return. Catastrophic gate; leaderboard tie-breaks are lexicographic with safety first. Roijers et al., A Survey of Multi-Objective Sequential Decision-Making, JAIR 2013; Hayes et al., A practical guide to multi-objective RL and planning, AAMAS journal 2022, arXiv:2103.09568 A scalar utility must be stated explicitly; linear scalarization assumes compensation between objectives; non-linear utilities express non-compensation. The score is an explicit non-linear utility: a product, plus a geometric mean for quality, so objectives do not compensate linearly. Fleming and Wallace, How not to lie with statistics: the correct way to summarize benchmark results, CACM 1986 For normalized ratios, the geometric mean is the consistent summary; the arithmetic mean of ratios depends on the reference. Quality is a weighted geometric mean of normalized ratios. Henderson et al., Deep RL that Matters, AAAI 2018, arXiv:1709.06560; Colas et al., How many random seeds?, arXiv:1806.08295 Results vary strongly across seeds; few runs give misleading conclusions; report variance and use significance tests. Multiple seeds per scenario, intervals, and an explicit "inconclusive" outcome. Agarwal et al., Deep RL at the Edge of the Statistical Precipice, NeurIPS 2021, arXiv:2108.13264 Point estimates over few runs are unreliable; use stratified bootstrap confidence intervals across tasks, robust aggregates, performance profiles and probability of improvement. Stratified (by family) two-stage bootstrap; median and tail statistics; paired comparison. Chan et al., Measuring the Reliability of RL Algorithms, ICLR 2020, arXiv:1912.05663 Report dispersion and risk (for example CVaR of the worst runs), not only the mean. CVaR10, p10, worst scenario and zero-score counts in every report. Bouthillier et al., Accounting for Variance in Machine Learning Benchmarks, MLSys 2021, arXiv:2103.03098 Randomize and pair sources of variance; compare with paired tests and a meaningful effect threshold. Paired episodes (common random numbers through the frozen fire); 1-point practical margin. Dror et al., The Hitchhiker's Guide to Testing Statistical Significance in NLP, ACL 2018 Use paired tests on the same test items; bootstrap is a valid non-parametric choice. Paired bootstrap over the same scheduled episodes. Efron and Tibshirani, An Introduction to the Bootstrap, 1993 Percentile intervals; stratified and multi-stage resampling for grouped data. Two-stage resampling (scenarios within family, episodes within scenario). Kruschke, Rejecting or accepting parameter values in Bayesian estimation, AMPPS 2018 A region of practical equivalence separates "statistically different" from "practically different". practical_difference = 1 point. Sokolova and Lapalme, A systematic analysis of performance measures for classification tasks, IP&M 2009 Micro averages weight large classes; macro averages weight each class equally. Macro (family-balanced) headline; micro and scenario-balanced reported as diagnostics (section 7). Rockafellar and Uryasev, Optimization of conditional value-at-risk, J. Risk 2000 CVaR is a coherent measure of the tail. CVaR10 of episode scores. Manheim and Garrabrant, Categorizing Variants of Goodhart's Law, arXiv:1803.04585, 2018; Skalse et al., Defining and Characterizing Reward Hacking, NeurIPS 2022, arXiv:2209.13085 An optimized proxy diverges from the goal; any scalar can be gamed unless its failure modes are tested. Adversarial policies and requirement checks (section 6). Helbing, Farkas and Vicsek, Simulating dynamical features of escape panic, Nature 2000 "Faster is slower": pushing at bottlenecks reduces the outflow. A bottleneck is charged by the outflow it loses: Time against a cut-capacity bound. The "jostler" adversary tests it. ISO 13571:2012, Life-threatening components of fire; the ASET/RSET concept of fire-safety engineering Exposure accumulates with time near the hazard; safety needs the required egress time below the available egress time. Hazard is a rate of avoidable danger-zone states; time is relative to the privileged earliest escape. Ouyang et al., An empirical study of the non-determinism of ChatGPT in code generation, ACM TOSEM 2024, arXiv:2308.02828 Outputs vary between identical requests even at temperature 0. Repeated trials; temperature 0 is not a determinism guarantee. 3. Design principles and how each is met Principle Mechanism Failure-sensitive multiplicative form; a zero component gives 0 Every component in [0, 1]; no bonus above 1 each component is a privileged bound over the actual value, or a probability-like factor Safety dominates Safety multiplies Quality; an avoidable casualty caps the episode below 60; beta makes every run without loss and without a severe failure score above a perfect run with one casualty (R12) Time and quality still matter below the thresholds Quality is continuous (Time 0.5 costs 22.5 points); severe failures cap the score below 80 (R2, R13, R14) A casualty hurts more than a success helps incident factor 0.6 on the first casualty; the last evacuee adds at most 1 - (1 - 1/M*)^2 Multiple casualties progressively worse the incident factor is paid again at every doubling of 1 + c, and the rate term grows Stranding and incomplete evacuation independent separate P_stranding and E Trajectory invariance every input is a function of the replayed state trajectory, never of the action log alone (R16; the block-scrub adversary gains exactly 0) Bottlenecks charged by their realized effect a severe realized bottleneck is a severe Time failure (T < 1/2 against Q_cut); its exposure and losses are in Hazard and Safety; blocked actions are diagnostics Difficulty-relative time T = Q_cut / sum(A_i) with the exit- and cut-capacity bound over the privileged earliest escapes, so unavoidable queues at exits and doors are not charged; severe below 1/2 Exposure penalized without deaths H counts danger-zone states of evacuees above their privileged minimum; severe above 1/4 Bad routing penalized P against the fire-aware privileged minimum of moves Failure to replan penalized R on route-invalidation events, plus the losses in Safety; severe below 1/2 Invalid output, model failure and timeout never disappear scheduled episodes without a result score 0 and are counted No blind double counting Time, Hazard and Path use evacuees only, so losses are only in Safety; the blocked moves of people who later die are not an input; Path and Hazard are relative to fire-aware privileged minima, so necessary detours and unavoidable exposure are not charged; correlations checked (section 6.5) Cost separate tokens, money and latency are never inputs; they are in a separate OperationalRecord 4. Candidate formulas and why they were rejected Every candidate was scored on the same evidence (section 6). The full tables are in scoring-study-results.md. 5.1 Additive weighted sum 100 * sum(w_k * x_k) over evacuation, survival, stranding and the quality components. Rejected. One casualty in 100 scores 99.4 (R1 fails), 10 casualties in 100 score 94.4, and 50% losses still score above 0. The "abandon the farthest 15%" adversary is only 7.2 points below congestion-aware. A weighted sum lets speed and order buy back lives, which violates the Safety Gym and constrained-MDP view. 5.2 Plain product of rates 100 * (evacuated / N) * (1 - c / N) * .... Rejected. One casualty in 100 scores 99.0. A product of rates is failure-sensitive only when a rate is near 0, so isolated deaths in large crowds are almost free. It also fails R5, R6, R7 and R9. 5.3 Official form without the incident factor (alpha = 1) Rejected. One casualty in 100 scores 94.1 and one stranded person 96.1, so a run with a death keeps a "95-level" score. R1, R5, R6 and R7 fail. The rate term alone scales with the population; the discrete incident factor is needed so that the first loss is expensive in any crowd. 5.4 Arithmetic (compensatory) quality mean Rejected. Time 0.1 with everything else perfect scores 73 (R10 fails): a very slow evacuation is hidden by perfect coordination and path. The geometric mean keeps each component's failure visible, as Fleming and Wallace recommend for normalized ratios: it gives 42 alone (design A, section 5.9), and 8.5 with the severe gate of the official form. 5.5 Dose-based hazard (sum 1/d relative to the privileged minimum dose) Rejected. The first study run used the metrics exposure proxy. It has Spearman 0.87 with Time, so it counts speed twice. It also rewarded the reckless fire-ignoring adversary: Hazard 69.1 against 64.5 for congestion-aware, because a fast run accumulates less dose even when it passes close to the fire. The replacement is the avoidable danger-zone rate: states within 2 cells of fire above the privileged minimum, divided by the evacuee states. Its Spearman correlation with Time is 0.14, and reckless now scores below congestion-aware on Hazard (89.4 against 89.9). 5.6 Horizon-normalized time (W - A) / (W - L) W is the horizon, A the actual and L the lower bound. Rejected. It depends on the scenario horizon and compresses differences: with H = 200, L = 20 and A = 40 it gives 0.89, while the ratio L / A gives 0.5. A long horizon would make slow runs look good. Baseline normalization (A - random) / (best - random) was rejected for the same reason: the reference baseline changes the scale, and random scores 0 on almost every scenario. The degenerate cases of L / A are handled: L >= 1 for every evacuee (an exit is never a start cell), and with no evacuee Time is undefined, not 1. 5.7 Static path efficiency The metrics path efficiency uses the wall-only distance. Rejected as a score input: it charges a policy for a detour that the fire made necessary (first study: fire-aware 95.3 against static 100). The replacement bound is the privileged fire-aware minimum number of moves. It reduces that unfairness (fire-aware 97.3); the rest is the extra distance of the fire-aware baseline over the privileged optimum. Path has Spearman 0.48 with Time and the smallest weight (0.1). 5.8 Replanning set to 1 when nothing was invalidated Rejected. It would fabricate a perfect component and raise the scores of easy scenarios. Replanning is undefined there and its weight is shared by the other components. 5.9 How Safety dominates: designs A to F The first version 1.0 draft was 100 * Safety * Quality (design A). It has a safety ceiling (one casualty: at most 60) but not safety dominance: a safe run with Time below about 0.22 scored below a perfect run with one casualty in a large crowd. A pure lexicographic order fixes that but makes Time irrelevant. Six designs were compared on the same evidence and the same requirements (section 6.2, R1 to R15) and pre-registered orderings (section 6.3): Design Definition Fails Decision A multiplicative (draft) 100 * Safety * Quality R12, R14 rejected: a severe exposure (rate 0.3) still scores 89; Time 0.1 still scores 32 B hard ceilings A, capped at 80 when any component is severe R12, R14 rejected: a flat cap does not grow with severity, and A's dominance gap remains C safety tiers Quality interpolates between this Safety level and the next worse one R10, R13, R14 rejected: Quality moves the score too little; Time 0.1 scores 70 D lexicographic (epsilon 0.05) 100 * Safety * (1 - 0.05 * (1 - Quality)) R2, R8, R10, R13, R14 rejected: Time becomes irrelevant (Time 0.1 scores 97) E soft minimum weighted power mean (p = -5) of Safety and the quality components R1, R11, R12, R14 rejected: one casualty scores 63, and a severe exposure (rate 0.3) still scores 90 F constrained geometric 100 * Safety * Quality^beta * Severity none adopted Two variants of F were also checked. With the dominance floor set at the stranding factor 0.8 instead of the casualty factor 0.6 (beta = 0.32), Quality is flatter: Time 0.5 costs 10.6 points instead of 22.5, and a severe Time 0.4 scores 55 instead of 46. It meets R1 to R16 with the current weights, but only just (R2 asks for 10 points). It is not adopted: the official beta is the largest exponent for which R12 holds by construction (q_min ^ beta >= alpha_c), so it gives Quality the most influence that safety dominance allows; any smaller exponent is an arbitrary flattening. Plain products and additive forms fail the safety requirements (sections 5.1 and 5.2). Why F works: beta = ln(0.6) / ln(0.5) is derived from the casualty incident factor and the smallest severe threshold. Every run whose quality components are all at or above their thresholds has Quality^beta >= 0.6, which is above the Safety of any run with an avoidable casualty. So R12 holds by construction, in every population, not only in the tested cases. Below the thresholds, Quality is continuous and still costs points: Time 0.5 costs 22.5 points. At a threshold, the severe factor 0.8 * (q / q_severe) adds a step and a slope. A severe failure caps the score below 80 and keeps falling with severity, so a severe realized bottleneck, delay, exposure or replanning failure is a substantial, permanent loss (R13, R14). 5.10 Aggregate attribution of unavoidable losses The draft charged unavoidable losses to casualties first, from counts: c = max(0, C - U) with U = N - M*. Rejected. It transfers an "allowance" between people. If person a could escape but dies, and person b could not escape and is stranded, the draft gives c = 0: the avoidable death disappears. The official rule is per person (scoring.md, section 4.1). On the study episodes the two rules happen to agree (0 of 1248 episodes differ), but test_real_episode_person_level_attribution builds a real replayed episode where the draft hides a casualty. R11 checks the same case on synthetic evidence. 5.11 Exit balance and allocation regret A 50/50 exit balance is never a goal and is not scored. An allocation regret term (extra time over an allocation-optimal schedule) was considered. Not adopted as a separate term: the time cost of a bad allocation is already in T, because T compares with the capacity bound Q_cut, which is allocation-optimal at the exits and at every door-like cut. A separate term would charge the same seconds twice. Exit utilization stays a diagnostic. 5.12 Coordination: the metric contract Scoring 1.0 at commit ce5e322 had a Coordination component C = (1 - block rate)^2 (weight 0.2) and a severe gate at a block rate above 1/4. This section tests whether any Coordination component can be measured without rewarding a different action encoding of the same realized trajectory. Full tables: scoring-study-results.md. Invariant (adopted, R16). If two policies produce byte-identical authenticated state trajectories (positions, statuses and fire at every step), their core EMBER Score is identical. It is desirable because the benchmark claims to measure evacuation outcomes: the people, the fire and the timing are the same, so nothing the score is meant to measure differs. Only the action log differs, and the action log is an encoding choice. Block-scrub reproduction. The adversary adv-block-scrub runs congestion-aware-v1, predicts the public resolver, and replaces every move that would be blocked by a person (occupied, conflict, cycle) with STAY. The concepts. "Coordination" mixes eight things: Concept What it is Trajectory property? In the score? A attempted coordination / action intent which moves a policy asks for no (action log) no: the scrub changes it without changing the outcome B realized coordination outcome who leaves when, and who survives yes yes, as Time, Hazard and Safety C unavoidable capacity congestion queues that every policy must form at exits and doors yes no charge: inside the bound Q_cut D avoidable congestion queues a policy causes, for example everyone at one exit yes yes, as Time above Q_cut (and Hazard while waiting) E queueing delay waiting person-steps yes yes, once: it is part of person-time, so in Time F exit / cut throughput loss fewer evacuations per open slot than possible yes yes, once: lost throughput is extra person-time, so in Time; throughput is reported G conflicts that change the trajectory a contest that moves a person later yes, through its effect yes, through its effect on Time, Hazard, Safety H conflicts that do not change the trajectory a blocked move where STAY gives the same state no no So the score measures B to G through their realized effects, and A and H not at all. Blocked moves are not all bad: in a door queue that no policy can avoid, a move into the queue is blocked or not depending only on the resolver's order, and the evacuation is optimal either way. Why blocks cannot be scored. No lower bound. Each other component is a privileged lower bound over the actual value. The block count has no positive lower bound: the scrub reaches 0 on every trajectory, so "bound / actual" does not exist. Gameable at no cost. The resolver is public and pure, and its inputs are all in the observation. Any agent can scrub, with no change in outcome. Not defensible as decision quality. Keeping an action-based component would need the statement "a policy that predicts a blocked move and emits STAY is genuinely better than a policy that attempts it, even when both produce the same trajectory". It is not defended here: predicting the resolver's tie-breaks is knowledge of the simulator, not evacuation skill, and it changes no person's fate. Dead-person double charge. On the generated study suite, 598 of the 844 blocks of congestion-aware-v1 belong to people who end as casualties or stranded; their losses are already in Safety. G6/G7 remove these blocks, but the remaining blocks still fail points 1 to 3. Candidates. Each candidate is scored on the same evidence (study suites and held-out suite). G5-official is the adopted form. The natural trajectory-only definition is the avoidable waiting of evacuees: waiting person-steps above the capacity-forced delay, (T - m) - (Q_cut - L), where T is person-time, m cells moved, Q_cut the capacity bound and L the free-flow bound. Every term is a Time or Path input, so the measure is an algebraic combination of the Time and Path components, and it correlates 0.88 with Time. Excess person-time over Q_cut is T - Q_cut, a monotone transform of Time itself. Sensitivity study 6.1 Setup python tools/scoring_sensitivity.py plays 16 policies on three suites: the public V1 suite with the public development seeds 0, 1, 2 (30 episodes), a generated stochastic study suite: 16 scenarios on a 16x12 grid with 6 to 24 people, stochastic fire and a horizon of 80, from a public config and a constant test-only generator seed (20261020), with seeds 0, 1, 2 (48 episodes), and a held-out generated suite from the same config and a fresh, pre-registered generator seed (20261021), with seeds 0, 1, 2 (48 episodes). Policies: reference baselines: always-stay, random-legal-v1, nearest-exit-greedy-v1, static-shortest-path-v1, fire-aware-shortest-path-v1, congestion-aware-v1; adversaries built to game a score: reckless-fast (load-balanced shortest paths that ignore the fire), abandon-far (the 15% farthest people stay), safe-slow (moves every third step unless the fire is close), late-start (waits 8 steps), jostler (prefers occupied cells), herd (everyone to one exit), wanderer (sideways moves when far from the fire), hider (runs from the fire instead of to an exit unless an exit is close), fire-hugger (congestion-aware routing that prefers cells next to the fire) and block-scrub (congestion-aware with every person-blocked move replaced by STAY; section 5.12). The changes are among adversaries and greedy: greedy falls to 9.3 (it stalls in the held-out high-density layouts), reckless-fast falls from 4th to 7th, and abandon-far rises from 12th to 9th. Block-scrub: 48 of 48 identical state trajectories, 1211 blocks against 0, score delta exactly 0 (R16). Under the 1.0 score the scrub would gain +3.1 points there. Cut-capacity bound: Q_cut <= person-time in every one of the 1773 episodes with evacuees (all suites, all policies); Q_cut > Q_exit in 104 generated and 60 held-out episodes, never on the public suite. Severe gates (any): congestion-aware 12.5%, fire-aware 16.7%, static 12.5%; Time is never severe for a moving baseline. 7.
